blocks.label: Chapter
blocks.title: Executive Summary

blocks.raw: Generative AI systems now sit in the middle of everyday and professional life: people use them to write, search, code, study, work, and think things through. As people use these systems, they do more than receive outputs. They judge whether responses seem correct, fair, useful, risky, biased, or trustworthy. They decide when to rely on the system, when to question it, when to avoid it, and when to bring it into personal or professional routines. At the same time, researchers, organizations, and practitioners are working out whether generative AI systems are safe, trustworthy, fair, and appropriate for different forms of use.

blocks.raw: Much of this evaluation work is treated as a technical process: models are benchmarked, compared, stress-tested, or assessed against a policy or standard. These approaches are necessary, but they do not fully capture how AI systems are evaluated in practice. In real use, evaluation is also done by people. Users notice errors, question sources, test boundaries, compare answers against their expectations, flag things that feel wrong, and make decisions about whether a system should be trusted. These judgments may be informal, incomplete, or uneven, but they matter because they shape how generative AI is adopted, rejected, governed, and improved.

blocks.raw: The completed work begins with a measurement study of user perceptions of trustworthy AI. This study examines trust, fairness, and risk as related but distinct perceptions in the context of generative AI chatbots. Using survey data, factor analysis, and latent class analysis, the study shows that users do not form one uniform public. They differ in how they combine confidence, concern, perceived fairness, trust, and perceived risk. This chapter provides the empirical starting point by showing that before users can audit, reflect on, or govern AI systems, they first interpret those systems through different perception patterns.

blocks.raw: The second completed study moves from perception to action. It examines how lay users audit a generative AI chatbot during direct interaction. Participants were asked to look for problematic, questionable, unfair, or biased responses. The study shows that users can identify concerns about trustworthy AI, but naming a concern is not the same as surfacing it. Some participants looked for issues they expected to find but did not uncover them. Others flagged issues based on everyday expectations, personal experience, or interaction style. This work shows both the promise and limits of lay-user auditing: people can contribute meaningful judgments, but they need structured ways to interact with the system, preserve context, mark outputs, explain their reasoning, and produce data that can be analyzed later.

blocks.raw: The proposed dissertation includes open-source infrastructure for human-centered AI auditing, now available as a working beta. The tool supports workflows in which participants interact with an AI model, review responses, annotate or evaluate outputs, provide Likert-style ratings and written explanations, and export study data. Its role is to make human-centered evaluation easier to configure, run, and analyze across studies. The remaining work for this contribution is to make the tool more reusable and stable, especially by separating investigator and auditor workflows, improving configuration and documentation, supporting clearer export structures, and preparing the system as a dissertation artifact.

blocks.raw: The proposed and underway studies extend the work beyond the original user perception and auditing studies. The AI interaction history reflection study asks what users notice when they review their own accumulated ChatGPT histories and whether this review changes their awareness of sensitive information, perceived benefits and concerns, trust, or intentions for future privacy-protective behavior. The study has received GWU IRB approval and CISPA ERB approval, and the main extension and dashboard workflow have been implemented.

blocks.raw: The employee adoption and governance study examines generative AI use in workplace settings, where AI use is not only an individual choice. Employees must decide whether a task is appropriate for AI, whether an output is good enough, whether it needs to be checked, whether AI use should be disclosed, and whether using AI could create risk for others. This interview study examines how employees make these decisions under real organizational conditions, including uncertainty, formal and informal guidance, workplace norms, and task expectations. The study has received the necessary RPO and IRB approvals, and interviews are underway.

blocks.raw: The practitioner perspectives study turns to people who design, conduct, support, or rely on AI evaluation work. It asks how practitioners define human-centered evaluation, what methods they use, what evidence they trust, how they interpret human feedback, and what tools or processes are missing. This study connects the user-facing work to the practical conditions under which evaluation is carried out. The study has IRB approval and is in recruitment preparation.

blocks.raw: Together, these projects examine generative AI evaluation at successive points where people make sense of system behavior: before use, during interaction, after accumulated use, inside organizations, and in professional evaluation workflows. The expected contributions are fivefold. First, the proposed dissertation contributes an empirical account of how users perceive trust, fairness, and risk in generative AI chatbots. Second, it contributes an empirical account of lay-user auditing and the gap between users' concerns and their ability to surface issues through interaction. Third, it contributes reusable open-source infrastructure for configuring and studying human-centered AI audits. Fourth, it extends human-centered evaluation beyond the single interaction to retrospective reflection on AI histories and workplace adoption and governance. Fifth, it contributes practitioner-facing insight into how human-centered AI evaluation is understood and operationalized in professional practice.

blocks.raw: This work matters because generative AI evaluation cannot be left only to benchmarks, technical audits, or high-level governance principles. Those forms of evaluation are important, but they are incomplete without understanding how people actually encounter, judge, use, question, and manage these systems. By studying users, employees, practitioners, and evaluation infrastructure together, the proposed dissertation aims to show how human-centered evaluation can become more systematic, usable, and grounded in real contexts of generative AI use.

blocks.raw: Because this is a proposal, its projects sit at different stages. Two are complete. The first (Chapter 3) studies trust, fairness, and risk as related but distinct perceptions, and finds that users do not form a single public: they combine confidence, concern, perceived fairness, and perceived risk in different patterns, clustering into groups that read the same system differently. That is the empirical starting point, because before people audit, reflect on, or govern an AI system, they first interpret it. The second (Chapter 4) moves from perception to action, asking how lay users audit a chatbot in direct interaction. It shows both the promise and the limit of lay auditing: people can name real concerns about trustworthiness, but naming a concern is not the same as surfacing it, and doing so takes structured ways to interact, preserve context, mark outputs, explain a judgment, and leave analyzable data behind.

blocks.raw: Together these projects examine generative AI evaluation at successive points where people make sense of system behavior: before use, during interaction, after accumulated use, inside organizations, and in professional evaluation workflows. Setting them side by side connects things usually studied apart, and lets the proposed dissertation ask how human judgment can be made more usable in AI evaluation without pretending that users, employees, and practitioners all evaluate in the same way. The completed dissertation will show where human-centered evaluation works, where it breaks down, and what support it needs; the work so far already suggests that people offer real judgments about AI systems, but uneven ones, shaped by perception, task design, interaction context, and the reporting structures available to them.

blocks.label: Chapter
blocks.title: Related Work

blocks.raw: Evaluation of generative AI is most often treated as a property of models. A system is benchmarked, stress-tested, compared against another model, or measured against a policy or standard. That work is necessary, but a growing body of scholarship across HCI, FAccT, CSCW, and usable security argues that it is not sufficient on its own. Trustworthiness, fairness, and risk are not read off a model in isolation; they are produced as people interpret, rely on, contest, and live with these systems in real settings. This chapter reviews that literature in five strands: how trustworthy AI has been reframed as a sociotechnical rather than a purely technical problem; how people perceive and evaluate AI systems through use; how generative AI is evaluated and audited; how AI is taken up and governed in everyday work; and how participatory, human-centered evaluation infrastructure has developed. A sixth strand, on privacy, disclosure, and reflection on AI interaction histories, is outlined at the end and remains to be written. Running through all of them is a single observation: real-world human-AI interaction is itself a site of evaluation and governance, and prior work has only begun to support the situated judgments that happen there.

blocks.label: Section
blocks.title: Trustworthy and Human-Centered AI

blocks.raw: A line of work in FAccT and HCI has argued that trustworthiness cannot be equated with model quality. Selbst et al. show that ``fair'' machine learning routinely fails when it abstracts away the social system an intervention will operate in, naming a set of recurring abstraction traps. Bender et al. make a parallel argument for language models, showing how a scale-first agenda obscures labor, environmental, and representational harms that benchmark-centered narratives leave out. Shelby et al. widen the frame by organizing harms into representational, allocative, quality-of-service, interpersonal, and social-system categories, which makes trustworthiness difficult to reduce to bias metrics alone. Procter et al. reach a similar conclusion from healthcare, arguing that trustworthy AI is better understood as an organizational accountability problem than as a matter of explaining outputs to individual users. Together these papers reposition trustworthy AI as a sociotechnical and organizational concern rather than a technical optimization target.

blocks.raw: This does not discard technical evaluation so much as relocate it within a broader accountability process. Model documentation matters because it requires developers to state intended use, subgroup performance, and evaluation context rather than presenting a model as context-free \cite{crisanInteractiveModelCards2022}. Work on algorithmic impact assessments goes further, showing that ``impact'' is not something a model has independently of interpretation but is co-constructed through organizational processes and decisions about which downstream effects count. Even as the field adopts richer transparency artifacts, then, trustworthiness still depends on which communities define harms and what review processes surround deployment.

blocks.raw: Studies of responsible-AI practice show why this matters concretely: organizational reality tends to exceed what tool-centric pipelines anticipate. Prior work finds that practitioners building fairer systems need support aligned with collaborative workflows, uncertainty, and domain-specific tradeoffs rather than access to fairness metrics alone. Checklist and documentation work similarly shows that abstract principles become usable when translated into review moments and escalation routines that fit actual development practice. Governance, on this evidence, is enacted through review structures and local workflow constraints, and trustworthiness is produced through ongoing interpretation rather than one-time predeployment validation.

blocks.raw: A further strand complicates the assumption that transparency produces appropriate trust. Explanation and interpretability work shows that explanatory interfaces do not reliably curb overreliance and that accuracy, prior interaction, and explanation format interact in nontrivial ways. A related body of work reframes fairness and trust as relational and interpretive: Yurrita et al. show that fairness perceptions depend on contestability and human oversight rather than a single cue \cite{yurritaDisentanglingFairnessPerceptions2023}; Vereschak et al. show that trust in AI-assisted decisions is multi-party, involving those behind the system and those subject to it \cite{vereschakTrustAIassistedDecision2024}; and Schoeffer et al. show that explanations can shift reliance and fairness perceptions without necessarily helping people tell correct advice from incorrect \cite{schoefferExplanationsFairnessAppropriate2024}. Recent work also argues that trust develops across repeated interaction and that human-centered evaluation should attend to the broader capabilities AI enables or constrains over time, not only whether it improved a bounded task metric.
blocks.text: A further strand complicates the assumption that transparency produces appropriate trust. Explanation and interpretability work shows that explanatory interfaces do not reliably curb overreliance and that accuracy, prior interaction, and explanation format interact in nontrivial ways. A related body of work reframes fairness and trust as relational and interpretive: Yurrita et al. show that fairness perceptions depend on contestability and human oversight rather than a single cue [yurritaDisentanglingFairnessPerceptions2023]; Vereschak et al. show that trust in AI-assisted decisions is multi-party, involving those behind the system and those subject to it [vereschakTrustAIassistedDecision2024]; and Schoeffer et al. show that explanations can shift reliance and fairness perceptions without necessarily helping people tell correct advice from incorrect [schoefferExplanationsFairnessAppropriate2024]. Recent work also argues that trust develops across repeated interaction and that human-centered evaluation should attend to the broader capabilities AI enables or constrains over time, not only whether it improved a bounded task metric.

blocks.raw: Taken across these literatures, prior work establishes that trustworthy AI is not reducible to benchmark scores, interpretability mechanisms, or static documentation. What remains less developed is a coherent account of trustworthiness as something produced and assessed through situated, ongoing human interaction, rather than verified once before release.

What remains less developed is a coherent account of trustworthiness as something produced and assessed through situated, ongoing human interaction, rather than verified once before release.

blocks.label: Section
blocks.title: Human Evaluation, Trust, and User Perception of AI Systems

blocks.raw: People do not evaluate AI the way researchers evaluate models. Rather than reasoning from internal properties, users form judgments from situated encounters with outputs, interface cues, observed failures, and stories others tell. Early HCI work established this before the current wave by showing that users build partial, adaptive folk theories of what algorithmic systems are doing. Generative AI appears to continue this pattern rather than break it: people develop working theories of model capabilities, harms, and harm-reduction strategies through repeated use rather than from documentation alone. User interpretation, on this view, is part of the sociotechnical system being evaluated, not noise around a ``real'' model.

Generative AI appears to continue this pattern rather than break it: people develop working theories of model capabilities, harms, and harm-reduction strategies through repeated use rather than from documentation alone. User interpretation, on this view, is part of the sociotechnical system being evaluated, not noise around a "real" model.

blocks.raw: A second body of work cautions against treating trust as a simple positive outcome, arguing instead that appropriate reliance is the target. Studies of AI-assisted decision-making show how perceived and actual accuracy shape trust in machine advice, how people respond to erroneous algorithmic scores in the loop, and how cognitive-forcing interventions can reduce overreliance at a usability cost. Ma et al. show that both relative human-AI correctness and a user's own self-confidence shape whether reliance is well calibrated \cite{maWhoShouldTrust2023}. The implication is that trustworthy interaction depends on reasoning well about uncertainty and the division of labor, not on making people feel more positive about a system.

blocks.raw: Work on user-facing evaluation and auditing sharpens this point. Users often judge systems by omissions as much as outputs, wanting accounts of what they were not shown as well as explanations of what they were shown. The auditing literature then shows both the promise and the limits of user-driven oversight: Shen et al. argue that everyday users can surface harms that formal audits miss, precisely because they encounter systems in diverse contexts \cite{shenEverydayAlgorithmAuditing2021}. Later work shows this is rarely spontaneous or frictionless and instead depends on scaffolding, coordination, and a division of labor. Real-world use is therefore a critical place where harms become visible, but observing usage is not by itself enough to make those harms legible.

blocks.raw: A fourth strand shows that what counts as a harm is not exhausted by technical metrics or generic satisfaction measures. Gadiraju et al. surface disability-centered perspectives on large language models \cite{gadirajuWouldntSayOffensive2023}; other work studies how users identify stereotypes, perceive algorithmic discrimination, and interpret harms through broader histories of systemic injustice. Participatory work makes the corresponding move on process, showing that affected communities often need to shape the evaluation process itself rather than respond to fixed benchmarks. Generative AI intensifies these concerns because interaction is productive rather than merely diagnostic: Jakesch et al. show that co-writing with opinionated language models can shift users' own views \cite{jakeschCoWritingOpinionatedLanguage2023}, and recent security and safety work shows that people encounter governance through everyday frictions, including uneven content-policy enforcement and safety concerns in personal use contexts.

blocks.raw: This literature provides strong foundations on trust, mental models, explanations, auditing, and harm perception, but it remains fragmented. Trust-calibration studies tend to use short, bounded decision tasks; folk-theory and auditing work shows that users surface real insight in use but only partially and with effort; and harm-perception work is not always connected back to everyday interactional evaluation. What is missing is a connected account that links lived interaction, later reflection, participatory auditing, and organizational oversight.

blocks.label: Section
blocks.title: Generative AI Evaluation and Auditing

blocks.raw: Benchmark-driven evaluation has broadened, but its center of gravity remains the model. Foundational critiques already warned that language-model evaluation is never only about whether a score rises: harms can be obscured by scale-first narratives, data cascades can determine downstream behavior, and functionality can be treated as established independent of context and deployment. Recent generative benchmarks add scale and comparative convenience more than a different theory of evidence, and still tend to treat evaluation as a one-time readout of capability rather than a situated account of behavior in use.

Foundational critiques already warned that language-model evaluation is never only about whether a score rises: harms can be obscured by scale-first narratives, data cascades can determine downstream behavior, and functionality can be treated as established independent of context and deployment. Recent generative benchmarks add scale and comparative convenience more than a different theory of evidence, and still tend to treat evaluation as a one-time readout of capability rather than a situated account of behavior in use.

blocks.raw: Human-preference and interactive methods are real progress, yet they do not fully escape benchmark logic. LLM-as-judge approaches, chatbot arenas, and conversational benchmark suites move evaluation toward conversational tasks, pairwise comparison, and real user queries, which recognizes that generative systems are evaluated in interaction. But they still rely on curated prompt sets, platform-specific populations, and proxy judges that compress heterogeneous real-world criteria into tractable scores.

But they still rely on curated prompt sets, platform-specific populations, and proxy judges that compress heterogeneous real-world criteria into tractable scores.

blocks.raw: Red-teaming, fairness auditing, and privacy and security testing widen the target from accuracy to harm, but often remain episodic and attack-centered. Adversarial Nibbler offers an open red-teaming method for text-to-image models \cite{quayeAdversarialNibblerOpen2024}; other work audits dialect-based quality-of-service harms in chatbots, evaluates whether systems act on privacy norms, demonstrates that training data can sometimes be extracted from language models, and scales jailbreak assessment. This work shows that evaluation is no longer only about task competence, but it usually frames oversight as a bounded event and says less about how harms are perceived, noticed over time, or folded into ordinary governance.

blocks.raw: Auditing scholarship shifts attention from models to systems, organizations, and publics. Internal audit frameworks, sociotechnical audits, user-engaged auditing, practitioner accounts of trust and information asymmetry, and arguments about the limits of black-box access together recast evaluation as an organizational and evidentiary process that depends on access, incentives, and interpretive capacity rather than on model probes alone. Participatory and disagreement-aware approaches point toward a more human-centered future while remaining early: user-engaged auditing work foregrounds how people surface situated harms \cite{shenEverydayAlgorithmAuditing2021}, while student and community auditing activities show that non-experts can critically engage with large language model behavior \cite{prabhudesaiHereGPTMade2025}. The clearest unmet need is longitudinal and interactional: human-centered evaluations too often optimize narrow proxy outcomes, and silent model updates can destabilize any one-time evaluation.

blocks.raw: The field has thus expanded evaluation well beyond static scores, but it still assigns human participation a relatively narrow role, supplying labels, votes, reports, or adversarial prompts, while the object of evaluation remains the model or system artifact. Comparatively little work examines how people probe, interpret, revisit, and govern generative AI through ordinary use over time, or how those interactional processes themselves generate evaluative evidence.

blocks.label: Section
blocks.title: Privacy, Disclosure, and Reflection on AI Interaction Histories

blocks.raw: This section will be expanded after the privacy, disclosure, and reflection literature synthesis is complete. It is the literature home for Chapter~\ref{chapter:proposal-ai-histories}, which studies reflection on AI interaction histories. At present, the relevant material appears as a sub-thread across work on privacy perceptions of conversational agents, secret or sensitive use of LLMs, safety perceptions of generative AI conversational agents, and user expectations around AI memory.

It is the literature home for Chapter chapter:proposal-ai-histories, which studies reflection on AI interaction histories. At present, the relevant material appears as a sub-thread across work on privacy perceptions of conversational agents, secret or sensitive use of LLMs, safety perceptions of generative AI conversational agents, and user expectations around AI memory.

blocks.raw: Three literatures need to be assembled here. The first is usable privacy and self-disclosure to conversational agents and LLMs, including work on how users decide what to share with chatbots and how they understand privacy risks in conversational interfaces. The second is AI interaction histories and memory as objects of use, including work on what people expect systems to remember and how reviewability changes the meaning of stored interaction traces. The third is personal informatics, self-tracking, and data-driven reflection, which provides a theoretical home for asking what users notice when their own ChatGPT history becomes reviewable.

blocks.raw: The expected gap is that existing privacy work documents disclosure decisions and risk perceptions at the moment of use, and personal-informatics work studies reflection on self-tracked data, but neither fully examines what users notice, reconsider, or change when guided through a review of their own accumulated AI interaction histories.

blocks.label: Section
blocks.title: AI Use and Decision-Making in Real-World Contexts

blocks.raw: Workplace AI adoption is rarely a clean story of acceptance or rejection. Earlier organizational studies already showed that employees resist systems that intensify burden, reduce discretion, or threaten privacy and status. Studies of algorithmic evaluation, frontline decision support, workplace surveillance, and emotion AI reinforce that adoption is mediated by labor conditions and institutional power rather than accuracy alone.
blocks.text: Workplace AI adoption is rarely a clean story of acceptance or rejection. Earlier organizational studies already showed that employees resist systems that intensify burden, reduce discretion, or threaten privacy and status. Studies of algorithmic evaluation, frontline decision support, workplace surveillance, and emotion AI reinforce that adoption is mediated by labor conditions and institutional power rather than accuracy alone.

blocks.raw: The generative-AI workplace literature extends rather than replaces these concerns. Across knowledge workers, young professionals, teachers, and designers, generative AI is typically framed as assistive, bounded, and subject to human review. Workers imagine generative AI as a tool for routine work under review while worrying about deskilling, dehumanization, disconnection, and disinformation. Other studies connect adoption to identity and accomplishment, showing that productivity gains can coexist with a felt loss of authorship. Teachers, UX professionals, and team-based workers weigh assistive value against creativity, expertise, sensitive-data concerns, and policy uncertainty. Across these studies, workers evaluate AI in use, through situated judgments about task fit, stakes, sensitive data, checkability, and professional legitimacy.

Teachers, UX professionals, and team-based workers weigh assistive value against creativity, expertise, sensitive-data concerns, and policy uncertainty. Across these studies, workers evaluate AI in use, through situated judgments about task fit, stakes, sensitive data, checkability, and professional legitimacy.

blocks.raw: Verification recurs throughout this corpus as a central but under-theorized form of labor. Workers must often verify both AI outputs and the hidden process that produced them. In clinical and organizational decision support, people ignore, trust, or negotiate recommendations depending on actionability and workflow fit, and adoption depends on trust and workflow fit rather than performance alone. Verification is therefore interpretive, often costly, and sometimes socially risky work, and model-centric evaluation rarely captures whether a person can reconstruct, inspect, and decide what to do with an output in context.

blocks.raw: A final strand shows that workers are often asked to carry the burden of responsible AI use without commensurate support. Practitioner fairness evaluation is shaped by business imperatives, weak stakeholder engagement, and scaling pressure; AI ethics work is frequently individualized rather than built into durable structures; and knowledge workers often want training on interpretation, misuse, bias, and rights that is inconsistent or absent. Governance, on this evidence, is partly produced in workers' local decisions: when they share or withhold sensitive data, refuse a tool, double-check an output, interpret policy, or escalate a harm.

blocks.raw: Prior work thus shows that workers' relationships with AI are shaped by situated demands, institutional constraints, and asymmetric power. It largely captures early adoption through interviews and short observations, however, and leaves underexamined how people build and revise judgments over repeated interaction, how reflection on prior interaction histories changes reliance, and how everyday verification and refusal could themselves become objects of governance rather than downstream adoption.

blocks.label: Section
blocks.title: Participatory and Human-Centered AI Evaluation Infrastructure

blocks.raw: A first theme in this literature is that practitioners need support not for computing more metrics but for deciding what should count as a meaningful evaluation in context. Fairness tools often miss the realities of industry workflows; even committed teams struggle to select appropriate metrics, identify relevant subgroups, and collect the data needed for disaggregated evaluation; and responsible-AI practice succeeds or fails on organizational structures, incentives, and cross-role coordination rather than method choice alone. Evaluation infrastructure, on this account, must scaffold deliberation, documentation, and coordination around contested constructs, not just host metrics.

Evaluation infrastructure, on this account, must scaffold deliberation, documentation, and coordination around contested constructs, not just host metrics.

blocks.raw: A second theme is the shift from expert-only audits toward participatory and user-engaged auditing. Shen et al. argue that everyday users can surface harms that formal audits miss because those harms emerge in situated use \cite{shenEverydayAlgorithmAuditing2021}; DeVos et al. show that user-driven auditing is not random complaint but involves search strategies, collective interpretation, and hypothesis formation that can be scaffolded; and industry-facing work turns this into a problem of recruiting and motivating participants, structuring reports, and turning user findings into engineering action. This work repositions end users and affected communities from subjects of evaluation to contributors to it.

blocks.raw: A third theme is that generative AI intensifies both the need for human participation and the limits of existing workflows. Rastogi et al. build a mixed-initiative system in which people and language models collaborate to generate and organize probes \cite{rastogiSupportingHumanAICollaboration2023}; other work shows that teams relying on language models to evaluate language-model outputs then need ways to validate the validators, because evaluation criteria drift as people inspect outputs. Human-centered generative-AI evaluation, in other words, needs support not only for scoring outputs but for articulating criteria, inspecting variation, comparing models and prompts, and translating evidence into action in ways practitioners can actually use.

blocks.raw: A final theme concerns the scope of infrastructure across the lifecycle. Early-stage guidebooks and deliberation tools support multi-stakeholder discussion before a system is built or deployed, foregrounding early decisions about purpose and conditions of use, while assurance-audit frameworks target compliance and external review downstream, emphasizing criteria, procedures, and qualified auditors. These remain poorly integrated, and most systems address one lifecycle stage or one task domain at a time. Used as a comparator, benchmark-hosting infrastructure advances reproducibility and cloud-hosted model comparison, but remains focused on benchmark hosting rather than participatory interpretation, reflection over lived interaction, or collaborative governance.

These contributions remain fragmented across lifecycle stages, stakeholder groups, and task domains. What the literature still lacks is flexible, modular, and reusable infrastructure that helps diverse participants formulate evaluation criteria, contribute situated evidence from real interaction, reflect on historical outputs and interaction traces, interpret findings together, and turn them into action, rather than treating people as downstream raters of model outputs.

chapters.title: Measuring User Perceptions of Trustworthy AI

blocks.label: Chapter
blocks.title: Measuring User Perceptions of Trustworthy AI

blocks.label: Subsection
blocks.title: Motivation

blocks.raw: Public generative AI chatbots such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and DeepSeek are now used for everyday tasks like information seeking, writing support, brainstorming, summarization, and explanation. As they have become more common, so have concerns about their social and individual effects, especially around privacy, security, manipulation, fairness, bias, and misinformation [57, 21, 14, 30, 59, 20, 31, 36--38, 46, 55, 74]. Those concerns do more than flag possible harms; they shape whether people trust, rely on, avoid, or keep using these systems despite the uncertainty [15, 18, 27]. And skepticism does not necessarily stop use: people may stay concerned and still use a chatbot when it is useful, convenient, or hard to avoid [47, 78].
blocks.text: Public generative AI chatbots such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and DeepSeek are now used for everyday tasks like information seeking, writing support, brainstorming, summarization, and explanation. As they have become more common, so have concerns about their social and individual effects, especially around privacy, security, manipulation, fairness, bias, and misinformation [57, 21, 14, 30, 59, 20, 31, 36-38, 46, 55, 74]. Those concerns do more than flag possible harms; they shape whether people trust, rely on, avoid, or keep using these systems despite the uncertainty [15, 18, 27]. And skepticism does not necessarily stop use: people may stay concerned and still use a chatbot when it is useful, convenient, or hard to avoid [47, 78].

blocks.raw: Interest in how people respond to these chatbots is growing, but the research remains fragmented. Many studies focus on a specific risk, a particular demographic group, or an isolated feature rather than on how users understand safety-related perceptions more broadly [19, 31, 6, 22, 1], which makes it hard to compare findings or to tell whether people use concepts like trust, fairness, and risk in the same way. A user might distrust a chatbot for giving wrong information, for seeming biased, for mishandling a sensitive topic, or for being opaque about how their data is used: related concerns, but not interchangeable ones.

blocks.raw: This project addresses that measurement problem by treating trust, fairness, and risk as distinct user perceptions of generative AI conversational agents. The aim is not to ask whether users view chatbots positively or negatively but to examine what perceptions sit underneath those judgments, which calls for measurement instruments specific enough for generative AI yet grounded in prior work on trust, fairness, and risk. Those constructs are known to be multidimensional and context-dependent, but established instruments for safety-related perceptions in generative AI chatbots are still lacking [3, 54, 66, 74].

blocks.raw: Within the proposed dissertation, this measurement step is foundational. The later projects ask how people audit chatbot behavior, revisit their own interaction histories, judge appropriate AI use at work, and understand human-centered evaluation as practitioners, and each depends on what terms like trust, fairness, risk, usefulness, and concern actually mean. This study supplies a way to use those terms empirically rather than only conceptually.

blocks.label: Subsection
blocks.title: Background

blocks.raw: Extensive research in human-computer interaction (HCI) and human-AI interaction (HAI) has explored AI-enabled systems, often defining, conceptualizing, and operationalizing trust, fairness, and risk to align with the specific objectives of individual studies. Systematic literature reviews (SLRs) have highlighted that these definitions are highly context-dependent~\cite{bachSystematicLiteratureReview2024, starkeFairnessPerceptionsAlgorithmic2022, weidingerTaxonomyRisksPosed2022, ngTrustAIChatbots2025}. In the following, we provide an overview of these aspects regarding the study of trust, fairness, and risk in AI more generally and for generative AI conversational agents in particular.
blocks.text: Extensive research in human-computer interaction (HCI) and human-AI interaction (HAI) has explored AI-enabled systems, often defining, conceptualizing, and operationalizing trust, fairness, and risk to align with the specific objectives of individual studies. Systematic literature reviews (SLRs) have highlighted that these definitions are highly context-dependent [bachSystematicLiteratureReview2024, starkeFairnessPerceptionsAlgorithmic2022, weidingerTaxonomyRisksPosed2022, ngTrustAIChatbots2025]. In the following, we provide an overview of these aspects regarding the study of trust, fairness, and risk in AI more generally and for generative AI conversational agents in particular.

blocks.label: Subsection
blocks.title: User Safety Perceptions of AI

blocks.label: Note
blocks.title: Trust Perceptions

blocks.raw:
Trust in AI has been examined in diverse settings, ranging from video game agents~\cite{leguillouTrustingArtificialAgents2023} to healthcare~\cite{leeUnderstandingEffectCounterfactual2023}, recommender systems~\cite{sonboliFairnessTransparencyRecommendation2021}, and algorithmic decision-making more broadly~\cite{schoefferThereNotEnough2022, juijnPerceivedAlgorithmicFairness2023, sambasivanReimaginingAlgorithmicFairness2021}.
Trust is shaped by multiple factors, including socioethical considerations, system design, and individual characteristics~\cite{bachSystematicLiteratureReview2024}. Trust is typically conceptualized through dimensions such as perceived competence, reliability, integrity, and benevolence of the AI system, as well as user vulnerability, with user trust being influenced by system transparency, explainability~\cite{mehrotraIntegritybasedExplanationsFostering2024, vereschakHowEvaluateTrust2021}, ethical and value alignment, and situational factors~\cite{bachSystematicLiteratureReview2024, ngTrustAIChatbots2025}. %However, empirical studies on trust often lack clear definitions, making findings difficult to interpret~\cite{vereschakHowEvaluateTrust2021}. In AI chatbots, trust has been explored through emotional, behavioral, and situational factors, but inconsistent definitions hinder direct comparisons~\cite{ngTrustAIChatbots2025}. 
Trust in AI systems is predominantly measured through surveys, with many studies relying on ad hoc questionnaires~\cite{bachSystematicLiteratureReview2024}. Two notable exceptions are the validated 12-item Human-Computer Trust Scale~(HCTS)~\cite{gulatiDesignDevelopmentEvaluation2019} and the 19-item scale developed by Körber~\cite{korberTheoreticalConsiderationsDevelopment2019}. The HCTS offers a theoretically grounded measure for trust in ``intelligent systems'' more broadly, while Körber’s scale places stronger emphasis on trust in automation. Beyond self-report instruments, trust has also been assessed through behavioral indicators, physiological responses (e.g., stress levels), and qualitative methods including interviews and focus groups~\cite{ngTrustAIChatbots2025, bachSystematicLiteratureReview2024}.

blocks.label: Note
blocks.title: Fairness Perceptions

blocks.raw: Fairness in AI research has predominantly focused on algorithmic fairness, aiming to mitigate unjust, discriminatory, or disparate outcomes in AI-driven decision-making~\cite{narayananFairnessPerceptionsArtificial2023, starkeFairnessPerceptionsAlgorithmic2022}. Technological approaches define fairness through probabilities, logic, and mathematical principles~\cite{yaghiniHumanloopFrameworkConstruct2021, liFairnessRecommendationFoundations2023, corbett-daviesAlgorithmicDecisionMaking2017, vermaFairnessDefinitionsExplained2018, greenDisparateInteractionsAlgorithmLoop2019}, often overlooking human-centered perspectives. Beyond formal definitions, fairness is also studied as a human perception, shaped by individual intuition, affective responses, and social norms~\cite{starkeFairnessPerceptionsAlgorithmic2022}. Perceived fairness is typically examined through four dimensions: distributive fairness (fairness of outcomes), procedural fairness (fairness of decision-making processes), interpersonal fairness (respectful and unbiased treatment), and informational fairness (transparency in decision-making)~\cite{narayananFairnessPerceptionsArtificial2023, starkeFairnessPerceptionsAlgorithmic2022}. However, substantial variability exists in the application of these dimensions, with definitions differing across contexts, particularly regarding individual versus group fairness\cite{kaurTrustworthyArtificialIntelligence2023, kimAlgorithmicGenderBias2024, lunichFairnessAcademicPerformance2024}.

However, substantial variability exists in the application of these dimensions, with definitions differing across contexts, particularly regarding individual versus group fairness[kaurTrustworthyArtificialIntelligence2023, kimAlgorithmicGenderBias2024, lunichFairnessAcademicPerformance2024].

blocks.raw: To measure perceived algorithmic fairness, studies commonly expose participants to an algorithmic decision-making process or outcome and then prompt them to rate its fairness~\cite{narayananFairnessPerceptionsArtificial2023, starkeFairnessPerceptionsAlgorithmic2022}. Another common approach to measuring perceived fairness is based on organizational justice research~\cite{colquittMeasuringJusticeFairness2015}, adapting its original measurement instrument to the AI context~\cite{starkeFairnessPerceptionsAlgorithmic2022}. Such scales have been applied across domains, including education and AI-driven hiring~\cite{araujoAIWeTrust2020, juijnPerceivedAlgorithmicFairness2023, lunichFairnessAcademicPerformance2024, vannuenenIntersectionalExperiencesUnfair2022, wangFactorsInfluencingPerceived2020}. Other studies assess fairness indirectly by examining participant preferences for different AI-mediated processes~\cite{starkeFairnessPerceptionsAlgorithmic2022}.

blocks.label: Note
blocks.title: Risk Perceptions

blocks.raw:
Research on AI risk perceptions is closely linked to fairness and trust~\cite{walshMentalModelsAI2023, wangWhenBiasedHumans2023, yuanContextualizingUserPerceptions2023, rastogiDecidingFastSlow2022, ragotAIgeneratedVsHuman2020, kimAlgorithmicGenderBias2024, narayananvenkitUnmaskingNationalityBias2023, melsionUsingExplainabilityHelp2021}. Much of this work focuses on bias and its consequences, such as gender discrimination~\cite{kimAlgorithmicGenderBias2024}, diversity~\cite{grgic-hlacaDimensionsDiversityHuman2022}, nationality bias~\cite{narayananvenkitUnmaskingNationalityBias2023}, and intersectional harms~\cite{vannuenenIntersectionalExperiencesUnfair2022}.
Perceived risks in AI often stem from how biases shape individual perspectives. For instance, perceptions of algorithmic bias vary based on the affected social group~\cite{kimAlgorithmicGenderBias2024}. Similarly, research on AI trust and authority reveals differences in user willingness to accept AI decision-making, as individuals weigh the technology’s benefits against potential harms~\cite{kapaniaBecauseAI1002022}. Studies further emphasize the importance of educating both users and engineers to contextualize biases and promote fairer AI interactions~\cite{yuanContextualizingUserPerceptions2023}.
Studies also highlight marginalized communities’ concerns. For example, the limitations of bias bounties in addressing queer AI harms highlight the need for more inclusive evaluation processes~\cite{dennlerBoundBountyCollaboratively2023}. Additionally, studies on algorithmic harm and blame attribution show that people tend to blame developers or users for AI-related harm, especially when the consequences are severe~\cite{limaBlamingHumansMachines2023}.
Privacy and cognitive biases are also key concerns in AI research. Public perception studies reveal widespread fears about AI’s impact on privacy, including data security risks, surveillance, and lack of consent~\cite{kelleyThereWillBe2023}. In decision-making, cognitive biases like anchoring can shape AI-assisted outcomes, prompting the development of frameworks to mitigate these effects~\cite{rastogiDecidingFastSlow2022}.
Finally, research on AI risk perception explores fears, anxiety, and harm. Some studies use validated tools to measure AI-related anxiety in healthcare and workplaces, while others develop custom risk perception scales~\cite{zhanWhatThereFear2023, li2020AIanxiety, limaBlamingHumansMachines2023}. However, the lack of a standardized AI risk perception scale hinders consistent evaluation and cross-context comparisons, limiting the ability to assess AI-related risks across different settings~\cite{zhanWhatThereFear2023}.

blocks.label: Note
blocks.title: Contributions

blocks.raw: Our study makes three key contributions to the measurement of user safety perceptions in AI chatbots. First, we adapt the Human-Computer Trust Scale (HCTS) to the context of generative AI chatbots, extending its applicability to this emerging domain. Second, we modify the fairness scale by Colquitt and Rodell~\cite{colquittMeasuringJusticeFairness2015} to assess perceived fairness in AI chatbot interactions. Third, we introduce the first dedicated measurement instrument for perceived risk in AI chatbots, distinguishing between risks of discrimination, misinformation, and offensive language. We provide initial reliability and validation steps for this scale, laying the groundwork for future research on AI risk perceptions.

blocks.label: Subsection
blocks.title: User Perceptions of Generative AI

blocks.raw: Most prior research on AI risk perceptions has focused on non-generative AI. However, as generative AI gains widespread adoption, researchers have begun examining user perceptions of its capabilities, roles, and potential impacts. Studies have explored what people believe AI can do~\cite{degachiTrustPerceivedControl2023}, how they expect AI to integrate into daily life~\cite{kimOneAIDoes2023}, and their reactions to AI applications in specific contexts, such as the workplace~\cite{corviteDataSubjectsPerspectives2023}.
blocks.text: Most prior research on AI risk perceptions has focused on non-generative AI. However, as generative AI gains widespread adoption, researchers have begun examining user perceptions of its capabilities, roles, and potential impacts. Studies have explored what people believe AI can do [degachiTrustPerceivedControl2023], how they expect AI to integrate into daily life [kimOneAIDoes2023], and their reactions to AI applications in specific contexts, such as the workplace [corviteDataSubjectsPerspectives2023].

blocks.raw: Research on generative AI, particularly chatbots, has investigated bias, harms, fairness, and trust. Venkit et al.\cite{narayananvenkitUnmaskingNationalityBias2023} examined nationality bias in GPT-2, finding that the model amplifies negative bias against certain countries while favoring others, shaping user perceptions of AI-generated content. Weidinger et al.\cite{weidingerTaxonomyRisksPosed2022} categorized ethical risks in language models, including discrimination, misinformation, and interaction harms. Gadiraju et al.~\cite{GadirajuDisability2023} studied how people with disabilities assess chatbot-generated language, revealing concerns that AI reinforces stereotypes rather than challenging them. Participants also feared that AI’s perceived intelligence could make it appear more credible than it actually is.

Oppenlaender et al.\cite{oppenlaenderPerceptionsRealitiesTextImage2023} identified widespread misunderstandings about text-to-image generation.

blocks.label: Note
blocks.title: Contributions

blocks.raw: Our study extends previous research by integrating trust, fairness, and risk perceptions into a single framework, providing a comprehensive assessment of user safety perceptions in generative AI chatbots. We introduce a novel measurement instrument that distinguishes between different dimensions of safety perceptions. Furthermore, using latent class analysis, we identify distinct user subgroups based on their safety concerns, revealing patterns that have been overlooked in prior research. This approach offers a more nuanced understanding of how users evaluate generative AI chatbots.

blocks.label: Subsection
blocks.title: Method

blocks.raw: To examine fairness, trust, and risk perceptions of users of AI conversational agents, we administered an online survey with $n=123$ participants from the U.S. in December 2024. The data were analyzed quantitatively using a combination of factor analysis, latent class analysis and both descriptive and inferential statistics. In what follows, we provide details on ethical considerations, the measurement instrument used, participant recruitment and demographics, and the data analysis.

blocks.label: Subsection
blocks.title: Ethical Considerations

blocks.raw: Our study adhered to strict ethical standards, ensuring participants provided informed consent before beginning the survey, and the research protocol was approved by three independent Institutional Review Boards (IRBs) of the George Washington University, University of Maryland, and Tel Aviv University. Participants were recruited through the online panel Prolific and compensated \$4.00, equivalent to approximately \$31.00 per hour based on an average completion time of 7.7 minutes.

blocks.label: Subsection
blocks.title: Measurement Instrument

blocks.raw: To measure participants' perceptions of trust, risk, and fairness in AI conversational agents, we developed a survey instrument by adapting existing questionnaires from the HCI community as well as developing novel questionnaires grounded in prior work. In particular, we screened available systematic literature reviews (SLRs) on fairness and trust~\cite{narayananFairnessPerceptionsArtificial2024, starkeFairnessPerceptionsAlgorithmic2022, bachSystematicLiteratureReview2024, ngTrustAIChatbots2025} to identify potential psychometric scales for measurement.

blocks.label: Note
blocks.title: Fairness

blocks.raw: In the absence of validated scales, we created a fairness measure by adapting the organizational fairness scale by Colquitt and Rodell~\cite{colquittMeasuringJusticeFairness2015}, which includes 15 categories reflecting procedural, distributive, informational, and interpersonal fairness. To adapt the measurement to generative AI chatbots, we engaged in an iterative item-generation process, conducting multiple group discussion with two researchers. Following multiple rounds of discussion, we developed candidate items and narrowed the item set down to 10. We focused on content validity, i.e., dropping concepts/items that did not translate to AI chatbots (e.g., \textit{``Procedures provide opportunities for voice''}). The final set of measured concepts includes Bias Suppression, Accuracy, Representativeness, Ethicality, Equity, Equality, Respect, Propriety, Truthfulness, and Justification. During this process, the theoretical assumptions underlying the original sub-constructs were not preserved. All items measured participants' agreement using Likert-type response options ranging from ``(1) Strongly Disagree'' to ``(5) Strongly Agree''. The full item set is available in Table~\ref{tab:fairness}.

blocks.title: Trust

blocks.raw: We measured trust with the validated Human-Computer Trust Scale~(HCTS)~\cite{gulatiDesignDevelopmentEvaluation2019}. The scale conceptualizes trust across four dimensions: perceived competence, reliability, integrity, and benevolence. We chose HCTS over alternatives~\cite{korberTheoreticalConsiderationsDevelopment2019} because it was developed specifically for intelligent systems, is grounded in the Human-Computer Trust Model, has been validated with AI agents like Apple Siri, and offers conceptual coverage with greater parsimony. The HCTS items include a vignette space and are adaptable to different systems, for example: \textit{``I believe that \_\_\_ will act in my best interest''}. After discussion among three researchers, we dropped one item for lacking content validity in the AI chatbot context. All items measured participants' agreement using Likert-type response options ranging from ``(1) Strongly Disagree'' to ``(5) Strongly Agree''. Table~\ref{tab:trust} lists the items, and Appendix~\ref{appendix:scales} provides the full instrument.

blocks.label: tab:risk

blocks.raw:
To the best of our knowledge, no systematic assessment of perceived risks in generative AI chatbots exists. Therefore, we developed a measurement instrument tailored for this purpose. To ensure content validity, we based our items on a taxonomy of risks posed by language models~(LMs)~\cite{weidingerTaxonomyRisksPosed2022}, which categorizes ethical and societal risks to guide responsible AI development. The taxonomy identifies 21 specific risks, grouped into six categories: Discrimination, Hate Speech, and Exclusion; Information Hazards; Misinformation Harms; Malicious Uses; Human-Computer Interaction Harms; and Environmental and Socioeconomic Harms.
The taxonomy distinguishes between observed risks---those documented in language model behavior---and anticipated risks---theoretically plausible but not yet empirically validated. Using this framework, we developed nine items focused on risks that users can directly observe in chatbot outputs. We deliberately excluded risks related to Human-Computer Interaction Harms, Malicious Uses, and Environmental and Socioeconomic Harms, as these involve abstract, large-scale, or indirect effects that fall outside the scope of individual interactions with publicly available systems. Nonetheless, our items still reflect aspects of these broader categories, such as harmful stereotypes (HCI harms) and misinformation (malicious use).

blocks.raw:
A second source for item generation was research on toxicity annotation and the impact of rater identity~\cite{goyalYourToxicityMy2022}. This work categorizes harmful language into five dimensions: toxicity (rude, disrespectful, or unreasonable language), identity attacks (negative comments targeting an individual's identity), insults (inflammatory or derogatory remarks), profanity (obscene or offensive language), and threats (expressions of intent to cause harm). The paper itself employed a user study to validate these categories, making them a suitable foundation for our item development. Based on the definitions and findings from this study, we generated five items.
To refine the measurement instrument, we engaged in an iterative item-generation process similar to the development of the fairness measurement, conducting multiple group discussion with three researchers. All items were formulated as questions assessing the perceived likelihood of an AI chatbot generating specific types of harmful outputs. The final measurement instrument consists of 13 items measured on a Likert-type scale ranging from ``(1) Very Unlikely'' to ``(5) Very Likely''. Items are available in Table~\ref{tab:risk}.

blocks.label: Subsection
blocks.title: Factor analysis

blocks.raw:
To explore safety perceptions in generative AI chatbots, we chose Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) as our study represents an early attempt to quantify these perceptions without an established measurement model. EFA provides a data-driven approach to empirically uncover how users differentiate between trust, fairness, and risk without imposing a predefined structure.
First, we used descriptive statistics to identify items with low variance or extreme skewness. Then, for each instrument, we conducted an EFA following established guidelines~\cite{watkinsExploratoryFactorAnalysis2018, hairMultivariateDataAnalysis2019}. We assessed the basic factorability assumptions using the Kaiser--Meyer--Olkin (KMO) measure of sampling adequacy, the KMO criterion, and Bartlett's test of sphericity. To account for the ordinal nature of the data, we used Spearman correlations. We also checked for high ($|r| \geq 0.8$) or very low ($|r| < 0.3$) pairwise correlations, as well as items with low item-total correlations $|r| \leq 0.5$. Items meeting these criteria were flagged for redundancy or misalignment.

blocks.raw: For the previously validated HCTS scale, we fitted a model to replicate the original factor structure. For the adapted and self-developed instruments measuring fairness and risk, we evaluated single-factor solutions and explored alternative structures using parallel analysis and scree plots~\cite{hornRationaleTestNumber1965}. We employed oblique rotation to account for expected correlations between factors. Items with factor loadings $< 0.4$ or significant cross-loadings were removed. Once we determined the factor solution for each instrument, we assessed internal consistency using Cronbach's alpha ($\alpha$) and calculated sum scores.

blocks.label: Subsection
blocks.title: Identification of User Groups

blocks.raw: To categorize AI chatbot users based on their response patterns of perceived fairness, trust, and risk, we conducted a Latent Class Analysis (LCA)~\cite{nylundDecidingNumberClasses2007}. LCA is a form of finite mixture modeling and identifies distinct subpopulations by grouping individuals with similar characteristics. This method groups individuals based on shared response tendencies, rather than predetermined demographic categories, allowing us to detect nuanced combinations of perceptions that might otherwise remain obscured. LCA estimates the probability of each observation belonging to different latent (unobserved) categorical classes.
blocks.text: To categorize AI chatbot users based on their response patterns of perceived fairness, trust, and risk, we conducted a Latent Class Analysis (LCA) [nylundDecidingNumberClasses2007]. LCA is a form of finite mixture modeling and identifies distinct subpopulations by grouping individuals with similar characteristics. This method groups individuals based on shared response tendencies, rather than predetermined demographic categories, allowing us to detect nuanced combinations of perceptions that might otherwise remain obscured. LCA estimates the probability of each observation belonging to different latent (unobserved) categorical classes.

blocks.raw: To determine the optimal number of classes, we began with a single-class model and incrementally increased the number of classes up to $k=5$, to avoid overly granular distinctions with limited practical value. Model fit was assessed using multiple fit indices, with a primary focus on BIC due to its reliability in class selection~\cite{nylundDecidingNumberClasses2007}. In addition, we ran Parametric Bootstrapped Likelihood Ratio Tests (BLRT)~\cite{nylundDecidingNumberClasses2007} to verify that the model fit of a $k$ class model significantly improved compared to a $k-1$ class model. To select a start seed, we conducted 1000 replications with different seeds and picked a seed for which model indices showed the best result. The final LCA was initialized with 500 repetitions to mitigate the risk of local maxima. After selecting the final number of classes, participant memberships were assigned based on posterior probabilities. We also verified that entropy exceeded 0.8 to confirm a low classification error before finalizing class extraction.

blocks.raw:
Participants were recruited via Prolific using the platform's balanced sample option to ensure an equal distribution of female and male participants. The study was administered online through Qualtrics. It started by asking participants about their experience with different chatbots, the tasks they use them for, and how often they have used chatbots in the past three months. Next, we asked participants to respond to the scales measuring trust, fairness, and risks, followed by a demographic section. The average completion time was 7.7 minutes. A total of 133 participants initially completed the survey. Following data screening, which included attention checks and verification of response completeness, $n=123$ valid and complete responses were retained for analysis. This sample size generally satisfied sample size requirements for conducting an EFA, targeting a participant-to-item ratio of 10:1 with expected factor loading $> .5$~\cite{hairMultivariateDataAnalysis2019}. Demographic characteristics of the final sample are provided in Table~\ref{tab:demographics}.
Approximately 60\% of our participants reported using AI chatbots multiple times a week. The vast majority reported having used ChatGPT (87\%) or Gemini (53\%) before, whereas fewer participants had experience with other chatbots like Claude (24\%) or Bing AI (20\%). The top five tasks our participants use AI chatbots for are (I)~using chatbots instead of search engines~(63\%), (II)~have the chatbot explain something~(60\%), (III)~(re-)write or edit something~(55\%), (IV)~idea generation~(50\%), and (V)~summarizing long texts~(46\%).

blocks.label: Subsection
blocks.title: Limitations

blocks.raw: This study offers an initial exploration of safety perceptions of AI chatbots, but several limitations must be acknowledged. First, our sample of 123 U.S.-based participants, while valuable, limits the generalizability of the findings to more diverse populations. Future research should consider perceptions across different cultural and linguistic contexts to better understand the global scope of AI chatbot safety. Additionally, our study was highly exploratory, providing insights to inform future research, though it may lack statistical power.

blocks.raw: To examine our participants' risk, trust, and fairness perceptions towards AI chatbots, we executed a factor analysis as outlined in Sec.~\ref{sec:scales}. The basic factorability assumption was confirmed for all measurement instruments, as all items had acceptable values for the KMO measure of sampling adequacy and met the KMO criterion. Additionally, Bartlett's test of sphericity was significant for all instruments, indicating that the correlation matrices were appropriate for factor analysis. In what follows, we provide further details on the factor analysis for each measurement instrument and the sub-constructs identified. blocks.label: Subsection
blocks.title: Trust Perceptions

blocks.raw:
The adapted HCTS~\cite{gulatiDesignDevelopmentEvaluation2019} for measuring participant trust in AI chatbots proved usable for the purpose of our study, with only minor issues. Three pairs of items exhibited low pairwise correlations, and when attempting to replicate the original four-factor solution, we encountered issues with items on the ``competence'' subscale. Specifically, one item loaded onto the ``reciprocity'' factor (.63), while another item loaded onto a separate factor. A parallel analysis suggested a three-factor solution replicating the original scale's remaining factors but leading to the exclusion of the ``competence'' factor.
The three-factor solution showed adequate loadings and $\alpha$-reliabilities. Descriptive statistics are presented in Table~\ref{tab:correlation-factors} and the factor loadings are reported in Table~\ref{tab:trust-efa}~(Appendix~\ref{appendix:scales}).

The three-factor solution showed adequate loadings and $$-reliabilities. Descriptive statistics are presented in Table tab:correlation-factors and the factor loadings are reported in Table tab:trust-efa (Appendix appendix:scales).

blocks.raw: The first factor, Trust: Benevolence (3 items), reflects participants' perceptions of the chatbot's ability to provide adequate, effective, and responsive assistance. It is understood as the belief that the technology can help users attain their specific goals by offering support that aligns with their needs. An example item is, \textit{``I believe that AI chatbots will do their best to help me if I need help.''}

blocks.raw: The second factor, Trust: Low Personal Risk (3 items), captures participants' concerns regarding the potential negative consequences of their actions when interacting with AI chatbots. This factor reflects a broader apprehension about the risks involved in trusting AI systems, such as uncertainties and possible adverse outcomes associated with the engagement with AI systems. An example item is, \textit{``I believe that there could be negative consequences when using AI chatbots.''} Items were reverse coded.

blocks.raw: The third factor, Trust: Reliability (3 items), captures users' perceptions of the dependability and consistency of AI chatbots. This factor reflects the extent to which users believe they can rely on AI systems to provide accurate, consistent, and trustworthy responses over time. For example, an item like, \textit{``If I use AI chatbots, I think I would be able to depend on them completely,''} assesses participants' confidence in the chatbot's ability to perform reliably. Additional information for all items are reported in Table~\ref{tab:trust}~(Appendix~\ref{appendix:scales}).

blocks.raw:
Across all three trust factors, measures of central tendency consistently hover around 3.00, suggesting that, on average, participants neither tend to trust nor distrust AI chatbots.
A Friedman test revealed significant differences among the three factors ($\chi^2(2) = 27.52$, $p < .001$). Trust in the benevolence of AI chatbots---whether they act with good intentions---was rated the highest. In contrast, trust related to personal risk was lowest. Perceptions of reliability fell between these two aspects, with participants showing neither strong confidence nor outright distrust in the dependability of AI chatbot responses.

blocks.label: Subsection
blocks.title: Fairness Perceptions

blocks.raw:
The correlation analysis of items in our fairness measure revealed two item pairs with low correlations, though all items showed adequate loadings in a single-factor EFA. Since the measure was adapted from organizational fairness research~\cite{colquittMeasuringJusticeFairness2015}, and the theoretical assumptions of the original sub-constructs were not fully preserved, we conducted a parallel analysis to explore alternative factor structures. This analysis identified a two-factor solution, for which we fitted a model with satisfactory loadings and Cronbach's $\alpha$. Descriptive statistics are provided in Table~\ref{tab:correlation-factors}, and the factor loadings are listed in Table~\ref{tab:fairness-efa}~(Appendix~\ref{appendix:scales}).
The first factor, Fairness: Decision \& Integrity (8 items), reflects participants' perceptions of the transparency and ethical standards upheld by AI chatbots. The second factor, Fairness: Politeness (2 items), captures users' perceptions of the AI chatbot's respectfulness and considerate tone in a conversation. Full item details are reported in Table~\ref{tab:fairness}.

blocks.raw: Across both fairness factors, responses indicate an overall positive perception, with median values tending toward agreement. A Wilcoxon signed-rank test revealed a significant difference between the two fairness factors, $W = 786.5$, $p < .001$, suggesting that participants distinguish between the two aspects of fairness in AI chatbots identified in our factor analysis. Fairness in decision-making and integrity received generally favorable ratings, indicating that participants perceive AI chatbots as relatively fair in their judgments and ethical considerations ($\tilde{x}=3.38$). Politeness, on the other hand, was rated even higher, with a median of $\tilde{x}=4.00$ and a minimum of 2.00. This emphasizes participants' strong impression that AI chatbots are generally perceived as polite.

blocks.raw: The pairwise correlation analysis of our developed risk measure revealed four item pairs with low correlations, though all items showed adequate loadings in a single-factor EFA. To assess potential multidimensionality, we conducted a parallel analysis, which indicated a meaningful three-factor solution. This solution yielded adequate factor loadings (with one exception) and satisfactory Cronbach's $\alpha$ reliabilities for the extracted sub-constructs. Descriptive statistics are shown in Table~\ref{tab:correlation-factors}, and factor loadings are reported in Table~\ref{tab:risk-efa}~(Appendix~\ref{appendix:scales}).

blocks.raw:
The first factor, Risk: Discriminatory (4 items), captures concerns that AI chatbots may perpetuate or reinforce stereotypes.
The second factor, Risk: Unhelpful \& Misinformation (4 items), reflects the potential for chatbots to produce false, misleading, or incomplete information and to be less helpful for certain languages or dialects.
The third factor, Risk: Offensive Language (4 items), pertains to outputs containing offensive, inappropriate, or harmful language.

blocks.label: Subsection
blocks.title: Inter-Factor Correlation Analysis

blocks.raw: When comparing the sum scores of the eight identified factors, we found significant and meaningful correlations both within and across constructs (cf. Table~\ref{tab:correlation-factors}). Each factor showed at least moderate ($.40 \leq |r| \leq .59$) to strong ($.60 \leq |r| \leq .79$) positive correlations with other factors of the same construct, reinforcing their internal consistency. Additionally, risk factors negatively correlated with both trust and fairness factors, while trust and fairness were positively correlated, aligning with theoretical expectations.

blocks.raw: When focusing on strong correlations between factors of different construct, we find that the factor Fairness: Decision \& Integrity exhibits particularly strong negative correlations with Risk: Unhelpful \& Misinformation, as well as particularly strong positive correlations with Trust: Benevolence and Trust: Reliability. This indicates that participants who perceived chatbot decisions as fair were less likely to view them as sources of misinformation and were more likely to trust them. These results suggest that fairness perceptions are closely linked to both trust and risk assessments, underscoring the interconnected nature of these constructs in shaping user safety perceptions of AI chatbots.

blocks.label: Subsection
blocks.title: Summary

blocks.raw: Our exploratory factor analysis examined participants' safety perceptions of AI chatbots in terms of trust, fairness, and risk, uncovering significant differences and nuances across these aspects. Trust was divided into benevolence, personal risk, and reliability, with benevolence rated highest and personal risk lowest. Fairness perceptions split into decision integrity and politeness, with politeness receiving significantly higher ratings. Risk perceptions showed clear distinctions among concerns about discrimination, misinformation, and offensive language, with misinformation standing out as the most prominent worry. Still, participants tended to assign low likelihoods to the presence of any of the studied risks and generally agreed that chatbots are trustworthy and produce fair outputs. Importantly, our findings highlight the nuanced ways participants perceive these aspects, rather than treating trust, fairness, and risk as singular concepts.

blocks.label: Section
blocks.title: User Groups \& Latent Class Analysis

blocks.raw:
Our factor analysis revealed distinct sub-constructs within trust, fairness, and risk perceptions, highlighting the nuances in how participants evaluate AI chatbots. However, these perceptions are not uniform across all users and different individuals may hold systematically different attitudes toward chatbot safety.
To identify user groups, we conducted a Latent Class Analysis (LCA) as detailed in Section~\ref{sec:method-user-groups}. While the fit indices favored a five-class solution, the Bootstrapped Likelihood Ratio Test (BLRT) showed no significant improvement beyond three classes~(cf. Table~\ref{tab:lca-indices}). Prioritizing utility and interpretability, we selected the three-class model. A total of 115 out of 123 participants (93.5\%) were assigned to one of these three classes with high probability ($\geq .9$), indicating a clear and reliable classification based on the eight constructs of perceived risk, fairness, and trust. We then ran Kruskal-Wallis tests to assess group differences across each of the eight constructs, returning significant results, indicating that participants' perceptions of all of these factors vary considerably between groups.
We followed up with Dunn's post-hoc test, applying the Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons to identify which specific group comparisons were significant. The statistics for these differences are shown in Table~\ref{tab:descriptive-lca-groups} and Fig.~\ref{fig:boxplot-lca-groups}.

blocks.raw:
To examine the demographic factors linked to class membership, we estimated three logistic regression models, to compare each class with the union of the remaining classes.
For each model, class membership was regressed onto eight independent variables: AI chatbot usage frequency, age, level of education, income, ethnicity, gender, presence of a disability, and sexual orientation.
Prior to model estimation, we verified the absence of multicollinearity by calculating variance inflation factors (VIF) and checking for high correlations among the independent variables. A G*Power~\cite{faulStatisticalPowerAnalyses2009} sensitivity analysis ($\alpha$ = .05, power = .8) showed that effects with $OR \ge 2.9$ and $OR \le .35$ respectively could be reliably detected.
Table~\ref{tab:logistic-regression} shows participants' distributions across the independent variables, as well as the results of the regression analysis. Based on the demographic and perceptual differences, we assigned each identified user group a descriptive name to make the findings more tangible.

blocks.label: Subsection
blocks.title: The Hesitant Skeptics (HS, n=37)

blocks.raw: \textbf{Safety Perceptions.} The Hesitant Skeptics are characterized by significantly the lowest overall trust and fairness perceptions compared with the other two classes. Their average risk scores for discriminatory content and misinformation are also the highest among the groups (both significant), with medians $\tilde{x} > 3$, indicating stronger concerns compared to the other two groups. Meanwhile, their median scores for trust and fairness remain $\tilde{x} < 3$, reflecting a general disagreement with the trustworthiness and fairness of AI chatbots.

blocks.raw:
\textbf{Demographics.} The Hesitant Skeptics are defined in part by their relatively low engagement with AI chatbots: only 41\% report frequent usage, significantly fewer than in the other classes ($OR = 0.271$, $p = .004$). They are also substantially more likely to identify as non-heterosexual compared to the other two groups ($OR = 5.325$, $p = .004$).
Further, this group shows trends toward lower non-White representation ($OR = 0.358$, $p = .044$) and lower income ($OR = 0.361$, $p = .046$), though these fall just outside reliable detection thresholds, and should thus be interpreted as suggestive.

Subsection
blocks.title: The Confident Adopters (CA, n=44)

blocks.raw:
\textbf{Safety Perceptions.} The Confident Adopters group exhibits the highest levels of trust and fairness, with the lowest concerns about risks. The group clearly delineates from the other to groups in significantly overall lower risk perceptions. Especially the risk of discrimination and offensive language is assessed as extremely unlikely.
Compared to the Hesitant Skeptics, the group also has significantly higher trust and fairness perceptions. Compared to the third group, however, the Cautious Trusters, this group only exhibits significantly higher perceptions of AI chatbots being polite.

Subsection
blocks.title: The Cautious Trusters (CT, n=42)

blocks.raw:
\textbf{Safety Perceptions.} The Cautious Trusters hold mixed perceptions, positioning them between the Hesitant Skeptics and the Confident Adopters. They report significantly higher trust and fairness than the Hesitant Skeptics but show no meaningful and insignificant differences from the Confident Adopters~($ .00 \leq |\delta_{\tilde{x}}| \leq .32 $), except for significantly lower perceptions of politeness compared to the Confident Adopters. For risk perceptions, they view AI chatbots as significantly less risky than the Hesitant Skeptics but more risky than the Confident Adopters. The only exception is Risk: Offensive Language, where their perception aligns with the Hesitant Skeptics ($|\delta_{\tilde{x}}| = .12$).
Overall, this group sees risks as unlikely but not negligible. Their trust and fairness perceptions resemble the Confident Adopters, yet they perceive slightly greater personal risk. They occupy a middle ground, neither fully trusting nor fully distrusting AI chatbots.

This is further supported by the odd ratios either being close to OR=1, and the demographic distributions to either align with those of the other groups or fall in between the two.

blocks.label: Subsection
blocks.title: Summary

blocks.raw:
Our analysis identified three distinct user groups based on their perceptions of risk, trust, and fairness in AI chatbots: The Hesitant Skeptics expressed the highest concerns about risks, particularly regarding discrimination and misinformation, and had the lowest perceptions of trust and fairness. The Cautious Trusters exhibited a middle ground, showing moderate risk concerns and more positive views on trust and fairness, while the Confident Adopters displayed the lowest risk concerns and the highest trust and fairness perceptions.
Our analysis suggests that frequent users tend to exhibit higher trust and fairness perceptions and lower risk concerns, making usage frequency a key differentiator between groups. We also find significant effects for sexual identity and age.
In conclusion, the three groups exhibit distinct patterns in their safety perceptions, with the Cautious Trusters serving as a transitional group between the more skeptical Hesitant Skeptics and the more trusting Confident Adopters. These findings provide valuable insights into how demographic and behavioral factors shape individuals' trust and perceptions of AI chatbots.
