chapters.title: Employee Adoption and Governance of Generative AI

blocks.label: Chapter
blocks.title: Employee Adoption and Governance of Generative AI

blocks.label: Section
blocks.title: Motivation

blocks.raw: Generative AI is becoming part of everyday work, especially in jobs built around writing, coding, analysis, and communication. Employees use these tools to draft text, make sense of unfamiliar material, organize information, or get a faster start on a task. But workplace use carries constraints that personal use usually does not: a prompt may contain organizational information, a wrong answer can affect a colleague's work, and a generated draft may need to meet professional standards. Even a routine task can raise questions of confidentiality, responsibility, and disclosure. [ ]
blocks.text: Generative AI is becoming part of everyday work, especially in jobs built around writing, coding, analysis, and communication. Employees use these tools to draft text, make sense of unfamiliar material, organize information, or get a faster start on a task. But workplace use carries constraints that personal use usually does not: a prompt may contain organizational information, a wrong answer can affect a colleague's work, and a generated draft may need to meet professional standards. Even a routine task can raise questions of confidentiality, responsibility, and disclosure. [ ]

blocks.raw: The rules for using generative AI at work are often less settled than the use itself. Employees may not know which tasks are appropriate, what information is safe to enter, how much they are expected to verify, or whether their organization wants them using these tools at all. In that gap they improvise, leaning on their own judgment, their read of the task, what colleagues seem to be doing, what supervisors do and do not say, and whatever formal guidance exists. [ ]

chapters.title: Practitioner Perspectives on Human-Centered AI Evaluation

blocks.label: Chapter
blocks.title: Practitioner Perspectives on Human-Centered AI Evaluation

blocks.label: Section
blocks.title: Motivation

blocks.raw: ``Human-centered AI evaluation'' has become a common phrase in research, policy, and product work. It usually signals that AI systems should be assessed with attention to users, stakeholders, harms, and the contexts of real use. What the phrase means in practice, though, varies with who is doing the work: one team runs a user study, while another leans on expert review, benchmarks, red-teaming, user feedback, or internal safety checks. People who agree that evaluation should be human-centered can still disagree about what that requires day to day. [ ]

People who agree that evaluation should be human-centered can still disagree about what that requires day to day. [ ]

blocks.raw: This study turns to the practitioners doing that work: researchers, designers, engineers, policy and governance staff, trust-and-safety teams, and others whose jobs touch AI assessment. The aim is to learn how they describe their own practice, what they are responsible for, what evidence they draw on, when users or affected communities enter the process, and what constraints shape the result.

blocks.raw: Taken together, the project chapters treat human-centered AI evaluation as a chain of practices rather than a single method. Chapters 3 and 4 establish the empirical starting point. The measurement study shows that trust, fairness, and risk are related but distinct user perceptions, and that users vary in how they combine confidence, concern, perceived fairness, and perceived risk. The lay-user auditing study then shows what happens when users act on those perceptions in an audit task, moving the work from perception to practice.

blocks.raw: The infrastructure contribution responds to a problem that surfaced in the lay-user auditing study: participation in AI evaluation needs infrastructure. The open-source auditing tool turns the study workflow, from interacting with a model through exporting analyzable data, into a reusable research artifact.

blocks.raw: The remaining tool work is organized by priority. The dissertation version does not need to be a general-purpose evaluation platform; it needs to be a stable, documented research artifact that supports this proposal's argument: human-centered AI evaluation requires reusable infrastructure for configuring studies, supporting participant evaluation, and preserving analyzable records of interaction.

blocks.raw: The highest priority is separating the investigator and auditor workflows. The investigator workflow handles study setup: configuring task instructions, defining questions, previewing the study, and preparing a version participants can complete. The auditor workflow handles participation: reading instructions, interacting with the model, completing the configured task, and submitting data without access to the setup controls.

blocks.raw: The remaining work has four parts: final survey refinement, recruitment and data collection, analysis, and writing.
blocks.text: The remaining work has four parts: final survey refinement, recruitment and data collection, analysis, and writing.

blocks.raw: First, the survey instrument will be shortened and finalized. The study already asks participants to complete a history review task, so the survey needs to keep the required measures without making the full study unnecessarily long. The final version will preserve the pre/post measures needed for the quantitative analysis and the open-ended questions needed to understand what participants noticed during the review.

blocks.raw: Second, recruitment and data collection will be completed. The study will recruit 200--250 usable participants after exclusions. Participants will be eligible only if they have used ChatGPT for at least six months. During the study, participants will complete pre-study measures, review selected parts of their ChatGPT interaction history through the study workflow, respond to questions about the review, and complete post-study measures and open-ended responses.

The qualitative analysis will focus on what participants report noticing during the review, how they interpret their stored histories, and what concerns, surprises, or management intentions they describe after seeing their histories in this format.

blocks.label: Section
blocks.title: Expected Contributions and Implications

blocks.raw: This proposal lays out a dissertation on the human-centered evaluation of generative AI, studied at several points of contact between people and AI systems. Its chapters run from user perceptions of trust, fairness, and risk, through lay-user auditing, open-source evaluation infrastructure, retrospective reflection on interaction histories, and workplace adoption, to practitioner perspectives on evaluation work. The connecting question is how people make sense of AI systems, and what support turns their judgments into something useful for research, governance, and practice.
blocks.text: This proposal lays out a dissertation on the human-centered evaluation of generative AI, studied at several points of contact between people and AI systems. Its chapters run from user perceptions of trust, fairness, and risk, through lay-user auditing, open-source evaluation infrastructure, retrospective reflection on interaction histories, and workplace adoption, to practitioner perspectives on evaluation work. The connecting question is how people make sense of AI systems, and what support turns their judgments into something useful for research, governance, and practice.

blocks.raw: The central claim is that human-centered AI evaluation is not a single method or study design but a chain of practices that runs from how people first perceive a system to how professionals design evaluations of it. The chapters trace that chain; the implications below follow it.
blocks.text: The central claim is that human-centered AI evaluation is not a single method or study design but a chain of practices that runs from how people first perceive a system to how professionals design evaluations of it. The chapters trace that chain; the implications below follow it.

blocks.raw: Chapters 3 and 4 already support the first link. The measurement study shows that trust, fairness, and risk are related but distinct perceptions: users do not approach generative AI from one shared position but combine skepticism, confidence, and concern in different proportions. Because system behavior is not read the same way by every user, evaluation methods that ignore these differences treat user judgment as simpler than it is.
blocks.text: Chapters 3 and 4 already support the first link. The measurement study shows that trust, fairness, and risk are related but distinct perceptions: users do not approach generative AI from one shared position but combine skepticism, confidence, and concern in different proportions. Because system behavior is not read the same way by every user, evaluation methods that ignore these differences treat user judgment as simpler than it is.

blocks.raw: The lay-user auditing study carries that finding into direct interaction. Users can identify concerns about AI trustworthiness, but auditing takes more than concern: it takes the strategies, context, interfaces, and reporting structures that let a person turn a concern into a prompt, a judgment, an annotation, or an explanation. If lay users are to contribute to AI auditing, the audit has to be designed around what they can realistically do and the support they need.

If lay users are to contribute to AI auditing, the audit has to be designed around what they can realistically do and the support they need.

blocks.raw: The open-source auditing infrastructure answers that need, and its contribution is practical as much as methodological. It lets a researcher configure an evaluation task, support interaction with a model, collect participant judgments, preserve the surrounding context, and export data for analysis. In the completed dissertation it will show that human-centered evaluation can run on reusable infrastructure instead of being rebuilt for each study. The investigator and auditor roles matter most here, because separating study setup from study participation makes the workflow clearer for researchers and participants alike.

In the completed dissertation it will show that human-centered evaluation can run on reusable infrastructure instead of being rebuilt for each study. The investigator and auditor roles matter most here, because separating study setup from study participation makes the workflow clearer for researchers and participants alike.

blocks.raw: Chapters 6 through 8 carry the work into settings where evaluation happens after use, inside organizations, and as professional practice. The reflection study examines what users notice when they review their own stored histories; it is expected to show how retrospective review can shift awareness, privacy concern, trust, and intentions for future use. It also reframes AI histories as more than logs of past prompts, treating them as records of what people attempted, asked, and were willing to entrust to the system.

It also reframes AI histories as more than logs of past prompts, treating them as records of what people attempted, asked, and were willing to entrust to the system.

blocks.raw: The employee study examines how AI use is negotiated at work, where evaluation is folded into ordinary decisions about task fit, verification, disclosure, and who bears the risk. It is expected to contribute an account of AI governance from the employee's side, showing how formal guidance, informal norms, task expectations, and uncertainty shape those everyday decisions.
blocks.text: The employee study examines how AI use is negotiated at work, where evaluation is folded into ordinary decisions about task fit, verification, disclosure, and who bears the risk. It is expected to contribute an account of AI governance from the employee's side, showing how formal guidance, informal norms, task expectations, and uncertainty shape those everyday decisions.

blocks.raw: The practitioner study treats human-centered AI evaluation as professional work, in which practitioners must decide what to evaluate, whom to involve, what evidence counts, how to read feedback, and how to communicate findings. It is expected to show where current evaluation workflows help and where they remain hard to apply, and to identify what tooling, documentation, configuration, and export support practitioners need from reusable evaluation infrastructure.

It is expected to show where current evaluation workflows help and where they remain hard to apply, and to identify what tooling, documentation, configuration, and export support practitioners need from reusable evaluation infrastructure.

blocks.raw: Taken together, the studies carry implications for AI evaluation research: evaluation should attend to the human processes around model outputs, not only to the outputs themselves. User perceptions, audit strategies, reflection after use, workplace constraints, and practitioner workflows all shape what an evaluation can show. A benchmark can establish whether a model performs well on a defined task, a red-team exercise can expose particular failures, and a policy framework can set out responsibilities; human-centered evaluation adds a further layer, asking how people understand, test, contest, and act on what a system does.
blocks.text: Taken together, the studies carry implications for AI evaluation research: evaluation should attend to the human processes around model outputs, not only to the outputs themselves. User perceptions, audit strategies, reflection after use, workplace constraints, and practitioner workflows all shape what an evaluation can show. A benchmark can establish whether a model performs well on a defined task, a red-team exercise can expose particular failures, and a policy framework can set out responsibilities; human-centered evaluation adds a further layer, asking how people understand, test, contest, and act on what a system does.

blocks.raw: The work also bears on responsible AI practice. Organizations that want responsible use cannot lean on broad principles or general warnings alone; employees and practitioners need concrete guidance on task boundaries, verification, disclosure, and risk, and ways to report concerns, document judgments, and connect human feedback to later decisions. Human evaluation that is collected but never made interpretable or actionable is hard to use in governance.

blocks.raw: For the design of AI auditing systems, a few principles follow. Evaluation tools should support the different roles in the process, preserve enough interaction context for later analysis, let people explain their judgments rather than only select ratings, and produce exports that researchers or practitioners can actually interpret. They should also be honest about their limits: a tool built for one kind of audit should not pretend to cover every evaluation need.

Evaluation tools should support the different roles in the process, preserve enough interaction context for later analysis, let people explain their judgments rather than only select ratings, and produce exports that researchers or practitioners can actually interpret. They should also be honest about their limits: a tool built for one kind of audit should not pretend to cover every evaluation need.

blocks.raw: The proposed dissertation has limits. Chapters 3 and 4 concern generative AI chatbots and specific samples, tasks, interfaces, and models, and should not be read as covering all AI systems. The later chapters add contexts but carry their own boundaries: the reflection study addresses ChatGPT users with enough history to review, the employee study sits within one organizational setting, and the practitioner study depends on whom it can recruit. These limits do not weaken the central argument, but they bound how far each finding travels.

blocks.raw: Each strand suggests further work. The auditing infrastructure can be tested in new studies, with different models, participants, and goals. The reflection study points toward longer-term work on AI history management, privacy controls, and user-facing review tools. The workplace study can extend across organizations with different policies, risk profiles, and cultures. The practitioner study can inform more detailed design of evaluation workflows, reporting formats, and tools that link human feedback to governance decisions.

The reflection study points toward longer-term work on AI history management, privacy controls, and user-facing review tools. The workplace study can extend across organizations with different policies, risk profiles, and cultures. The practitioner study can inform more detailed design of evaluation workflows, reporting formats, and tools that link human feedback to governance decisions.

blocks.raw: The broader aim is to make human-centered AI evaluation concrete. Saying that AI should be evaluated with people in mind is not enough; this work asks what that actually requires at each link in the chain, and argues that human judgment belongs inside the evaluation process rather than alongside it as an afterthought.

blocks.label: Section
blocks.title: Ethical Considerations Statement

blocks.raw:
Our study was reviewed and approved by the Institutional Review Boards (IRBs) at the George Washington University, University of Maryland, and Tel Aviv University. All participants provided informed consent before participation. Recruitment was conducted via the Prolific platform. Participants who completed the initial screener survey received \$0.90, and main study participants received \$10.69. All compensation was benchmarked to meet or exceed minimum wage standards in Washington, D.C., where the study was conducted.
To protect participant confidentiality, all data were collected using Prolific-assigned pseudonyms. The study was hosted on a secure, institutionally managed server. Meta's \texttt{Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct} model was deployed locally using the vLLM serving framework and was not connected to the internet. This ensured complete control over data storage and access. Participants interacted with the model through a custom, browser-based survey interface. To mitigate disclosure risks, a persistent on-screen banner reminded participants not to share personally identifiable information (PII) with the chatbot. Additionally, during qualitative analysis, researchers manually reviewed all conversation logs to redact any PII that may have been incidentally disclosed. We did not find any. No automated redaction tools were used, which informed the team's caution around releasing user-generated content.
The study collected sensitive demographic information, including gender identity and sexual orientation. For all such items, a ``prefer not to answer'' option was provided, and declining to answer had no effect on compensation or inclusion in the dataset. Participation was optional at all stages, including survey completion and chatbot interaction. Sampling was designed to reflect U.S. demographic diversity across variables such as age, gender, race, income, and political affiliation. While the research team did not explicitly assess or record its own demographic makeup, care was taken to present findings without overgeneralizing or reinforcing bias.

blocks.raw: The potential risk to participants was minimal, since Llama-3.1 was already publicly deployed by Meta, and our study did not expose participants to harms beyond those present in widely available commercial applications, such as the AI assistant in WhatsApp. Participants could choose not to disclose sensitive information and were never penalized for non-participation or withdrawal. We informed participants through recruitment and the consent form that the chatbot may generate sensitive outputs. We provided contact information to \url{https://findahelpline.com/countries/us} in case participants felt the need to talk to someone about their emotions. We did not disclose the model's name or vendor to participants, so trustworthiness perceptions were not linked to either Meta or their products.

blocks.raw: During the review of participants' interactions, the involved researchers encountered potentially offensive, biased, or disturbing content generated by users or models. Although the study did not include a formal assessment of the researchers' well-being, safety measures and structured analysis protocols were put in place to mitigate emotional distress and reduce the risk of exposure to harmful content. First, we made a conscious decision to design our study in a constructive scenario in which the chatbot was to be tested for problems, rather than framing the task in negative terms, which could have led participants to use explicit or harmful language. In addition, researchers collaborated closely with other researchers on this project and had the opportunity to discuss concerns as needed.

blocks.venue: International Journal of Bank Marketing
blocks.text: Bouhia, Mariem and Rajaobelina, Lova and PromTep, Sandrine and Arcand, Manon and Ricard, Line. (2022). Drivers of Privacy Concerns When Interacting with a Chatbot in a Customer Service Encounter. International Journal of Bank Marketing

fields.title: Drivers of Privacy Concerns When Interacting with a Chatbot in a Customer Service Encounter
fields.author: Bouhia, Mariem and Rajaobelina, Lova and PromTep, Sandrine and Arcand, Manon and Ricard, Line
fields.abstract: Purpose - This study aims to examine the antecedents of privacy concerns in the era of artificial intelligence. Specifically, it focuses on the impact of various factors related to interactions with a chatbot (creepiness and perceived risk) and individual traits (familiarity with chatbots and need for privacy) in relation to privacy when interacting with a chatbot in the context of financial services. The moderating effect of gender on these relationships was also examined.

blocks.author: Brown, Shea and Davidovic, Jovana and Hasan, Ali

fields.title: The Algorithm Audit: Scoring the Algorithms That Score Us
fields.author: Brown, Shea and Davidovic, Jovana and Hasan, Ali
fields.abstract: In recent years, the ethical impact of AI has been increasingly scrutinized, with public scandals emerging over biased outcomes, lack of transparency, and the misuse of data. This has led to a growing mistrust of AI and increased calls for mandated ethical audits of algorithms. Current proposals for ethical assessment of algorithms are either too high level to be put into practice without further guidance, or they focus on very specific and technical notions of fairness or transparency that do not consider multiple stakeholders or the broader social context. In this article, we present an auditing framework to guide the ethical assessment of an algorithm. The audit instrument itself is comprised of three elements: a list of possible interests of stakeholders affected by the algorithm, an assessment of metrics that describe key ethically salient features of the algorithm, and a relevancy matrix that connects the assessed metrics to stakeholder interests. The proposed audit instrument yields an ethical evaluation of an algorithm that could be used by regulators and others interested in doing due diligence, while paying careful attention to the complex societal context within which the algorithm is deployed.

blocks.author: Burnham, Kenneth P. and Anderson, David R.
blocks.venue: Sociological Methods & Research
blocks.text: Burnham, Kenneth P. and Anderson, David R.. (2004). Multimodel Inference: Understanding AIC and BIC in Model Selection. Sociological Methods & Research

fields.title: Multimodel Inference: Understanding AIC and BIC in Model Selection
fields.author: Burnham, Kenneth P. and Anderson, David R.
fields.abstract: The model selection literature has been generally poor at reflecting the deep foundations of the Akaike information criterion (AIC) and at making appropriate comparisons to the Bayesian information criterion (BIC). There is a clear philosophy, a sound criterion based in information theory, and a rigorous statistical foundation for AIC. AIC can be justified as Bayesian using a "savvy" prior on models that is a function of sample size and the number of model parameters. Furthermore, BIC can be derived as a non-Bayesian result. Therefore, arguments about using AIC versus BIC for model selection cannot be from a Bayes versus frequentist perspective. The philosophical context of what is assumed about reality, approximating models, and the intent of model-based inference should determine whether AIC or BIC is used. Various facets of such multimodel inference are presented here, particularly methods of model averaging.

blocks.title: The Influence of Mental State Attributions on Trust in Large Language Models
blocks.author: Colombatto, Clara and Birch, Jonathan and Fleming, Stephen M.
blocks.venue: Communications Psychology
blocks.text: Colombatto, Clara and Birch, Jonathan and Fleming, Stephen M.. (2025). The Influence of Mental State Attributions on Trust in Large Language Models. Communications Psychology

fields.title: The Influence of Mental State Attributions on Trust in Large Language Models
fields.author: Colombatto, Clara and Birch, Jonathan and Fleming, Stephen M.
fields.abstract: Abstract Rapid advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have led users to believe that systems such as large language models (LLMs) have mental states, including the capacity for `experience' (e.g., emotions and consciousness). These folk-psychological attributions often diverge from expert opinion and are distinct from attributions of `intelligence' (e.g., reasoning, planning), and yet may affect trust in AI systems. While past work provides some support for a link between anthropomorphism and trust, the impact of attributions of consciousness and other aspects of mentality on user trust remains unclear. We explored this in a preregistered experiment (N\,=\,410) in which participants rated the capacity of an LLM to exhibit consciousness and a variety of other mental states. They then completed a decision-making task where they could revise their choices based on the advice of an LLM. Bayesian analyses revealed strong evidence against a positive correlation between attributions of consciousness and advice-taking; indeed, a dimension of mental states related to experience showed a negative relationship with advice-taking, while attributions of intelligence were strongly correlated with advice acceptance. These findings highlight how users' attitudes and behaviours are shaped by sophisticated intuitions about the capacities of LLMs-with different aspects of mental state attribution predicting people's trust in these systems.

blocks.title: Toward User-Driven Algorithm Auditing: Investigating Users' Strategies for Uncovering Harmful Algorithmic Behavior
blocks.author: DeVos, Alicia and Dhabalia, Aditi and Shen, Hong and Holstein, Kenneth and Eslami, Motahhare
blocks.venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
blocks.text: DeVos, Alicia and Dhabalia, Aditi and Shen, Hong and Holstein, Kenneth and Eslami, Motahhare. (2022). Toward User-Driven Algorithm Auditing: Investigating Users' Strategies for Uncovering Harmful Algorithmic Behavior. CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems

fields.title: Toward User-Driven Algorithm Auditing: Investigating Users' Strategies for Uncovering Harmful Algorithmic Behavior
fields.booktitle: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
fields.author: DeVos, Alicia and Dhabalia, Aditi and Shen, Hong and Holstein, Kenneth and Eslami, Motahhare
fields.abstract: Recent work in HCI suggests that users can be powerful in surfacing harmful algorithmic behaviors that formal auditing approaches fail to detect. However, it is not well understood how users are often able to be so effective, nor how we might support more effective user-driven auditing. To investigate, we conducted a series of think-aloud interviews, diary studies, and workshops, exploring how users find and make sense of harmful behaviors in algorithmic systems, both individually and collectively. Based on our findings, we present a process model capturing the dynamics of and influences on users' search and sensemaking behaviors. We find that 1) users' search strategies and interpretations are heavily guided by their personal experiences with and exposures to societal bias; and 2) collective sensemaking amongst multiple users is invaluable in user-driven algorithm audits. We offer directions for the design of future methods and tools that can better support user-driven auditing.

blocks.title: Data quality in online human-subjects research: Comparisons between MTurk , Prolific , CloudResearch , Qualtrics , and SONA
blocks.author: Douglas, Benjamin D. and Ewell, Patrick J. and Brauer, Markus
blocks.venue: PLOS ONE
blocks.text: Douglas, Benjamin D. and Ewell, Patrick J. and Brauer, Markus. (2023). Data quality in online human-subjects research: Comparisons between MTurk , Prolific , CloudResearch , Qualtrics , and SONA. PLOS ONE

fields.title: Data quality in online human-subjects research: Comparisons between MTurk , Prolific , CloudResearch , Qualtrics , and SONA
fields.shorttitle: Data quality in online human-subjects research
fields.abstract: With the proliferation of online data collection in human-subjects research, concerns have been raised over the presence of inattentive survey participants and non-human respondents (bots). We compared the quality of the data collected through five commonly used platforms. Data quality was indicated by the percentage of participants who meaningfully respond to the researcher’s question (high quality) versus those who only contribute noise (low quality). We found that compared to MTurk, Qualtrics, or an undergraduate student sample (i.e., SONA), participants on Prolific and CloudResearch were more likely to pass various attention checks, provide meaningful answers, follow instructions, remember previously presented information, have a unique IP address and geolocation, and work slowly enough to be able to read all the items. We divided the samples into high- and low-quality respondents and computed the cost we paid per high-quality respondent. Prolific (\$1.90) and CloudResearch (\$2.00) were cheaper than MTurk (\$4.36) and Qualtrics (\$8.17). SONA cost \$0.00, yet took the longest to collect the data.
fields.author: Douglas, Benjamin D. and Ewell, Patrick J. and Brauer, Markus

blocks.author: Festinger, Leon
blocks.venue: Stanford University Press
blocks.text: Festinger, Leon. (1957). A theory of cognitive dissonance. Stanford University Press

fields.title: A theory of cognitive dissonance
fields.abstract: Cognitive dissonance can be seen as an antecedent condition which leads to activity oriented toward dissonance reduction just as hunger leads to activity oriented toward hunger reduction. [This book] explores, in a wide variety of contexts, the consequences of the existence of cognitive dissonance and the attempts on the part of humans to reduce it. . . . This book explores contexts ranging from individual decision situations to mass phenomena. Since reduction of dissonance is a basic process in humans, it is not surprising that its manifestations may be observed in such a wide variety of contexts. blocks.title: The Global Landscape of AI Ethics Guidelines
blocks.author: Jobin, Anna and Ienca, Marcello and Vayena, Effy
blocks.venue: Nature Machine Intelligence
blocks.text: Jobin, Anna and Ienca, Marcello and Vayena, Effy. (2019). The Global Landscape of AI Ethics Guidelines. Nature Machine Intelligence

fields.title: The Global Landscape of AI Ethics Guidelines
fields.author: Jobin, Anna and Ienca, Marcello and Vayena, Effy
fields.abstract: In the past five years, private companies, research institutions and public sector organizations have issued principles and guidelines for ethical artificial intelligence (AI). However, despite an apparent agreement that AI should be `ethical', there is debate about both what constitutes `ethical AI' and which ethical requirements, technical standards and best practices are needed for its realization. To investigate whether a global agreement on these questions is emerging, we mapped and analysed the current corpus of principles and guidelines on ethical AI. Our results reveal a global convergence emerging around five ethical principles (transparency, justice and fairness, non-maleficence, responsibility and privacy), with substantive divergence in relation to how these principles are interpreted, why they are deemed important, what issue, domain or actors they pertain to, and how they should be implemented. Our findings highlight the importance of integrating guideline-development efforts with substantive ethical analysis and adequate implementation strategies.

fields.abstract: Because algorithm audits are conducted by technical experts, audits are necessarily limited to the hypotheses that experts think to test. End users hold the promise to expand this purview, as they inhabit spaces and witness algorithmic impacts that auditors do not. In pursuit of this goal, we propose end-user audits-system-scale audits led by non-technical users-and present an approach that scaffolds end users in hypothesis generation, evidence identification, and results communication. Today, performing a system-scale audit requires substantial user effort to label thousands of system outputs, so we introduce a collaborative filtering technique that leverages the algorithmic system's own disaggregated training data to project from a small number of end user labels onto the full test set. Our end-user auditing tool, IndieLabel, employs these predicted labels so that users can rapidly explore where their opinions diverge from the algorithmic system's outputs. By highlighting topic areas where the system is under-performing for the user and surfacing sets of likely error cases, the tool guides the user in authoring an audit report. In an evaluation of end-user audits on a popular comment toxicity model with 17 non-technical participants, participants both replicated issues that formal audits had previously identified and also raised previously underreported issues such as under-flagging on veiled forms of hate that perpetuate stigma and over-flagging of slurs that have been reclaimed by marginalized communities.

blocks.title: Trustworthy LLMs : A Survey and Guideline for Evaluating Large Language Models ' Alignment
blocks.author: Liu, Yang and Yao, Yuanshun and Ton, Jean-Francois and Zhang, Xiaoying and Guo, Ruocheng and Cheng, Hao and Klochkov, Yegor and Taufiq, Muhammad Faaiz and Li, Hang

fields.title: Trustworthy LLMs : A Survey and Guideline for Evaluating Large Language Models ' Alignment
fields.booktitle: Socially Responsible Language Modelling Research
fields.author: Liu, Yang and Yao, Yuanshun and Ton, Jean-Francois and Zhang, Xiaoying and Guo, Ruocheng and Cheng, Hao and Klochkov, Yegor and Taufiq, Muhammad Faaiz and Li, Hang
fields.abstract: Ensuring alignment has become a critical task before deploying large language models (LLMs) in real-world applications. A major challenge faced by practitioners is the lack of clear guidance on evaluating whether LLM outputs align with social norms, values, and regulations. This obstacle hinders the systematic iteration and deployment of LLMs. To address this issue, this paper presents a comprehensive survey of key dimensions that are crucial to consider when assessing LLM trustworthiness. The survey covers 7 major categories of LLM trustworthiness: reliability, safety, fairness, resistance to misuse, explainability and reasoning, adherence to social norms, and robustness. Each major category is further divided into several sub-categories, resulting in a total of 29 sub-categories. Additionally, a subset of 8 sub-categories is selected for further investigation, where corresponding measurement studies are designed and conducted on several widely-used LLMs. The measurement results indicate that, in general, more aligned models tend to perform better in terms of overall trustworthiness. However, the effectiveness of alignment varies across the different trustworthiness categories considered. This highlights the importance of conducting more fine-grained analyses, testing, and making continuous improvements on LLM alignment. By shedding light on these key dimensions of LLM trustworthiness, this paper aims to provide valuable insights and guidance to practitioners in the field. Understanding and addressing these concerns will be crucial in achieving reliable and ethically sound deployment of LLMs in various applications.

blocks.title: Prevalence Overshadows Concerns? Understanding Chinese Users' Privacy Awareness and Expectations towards LLM-based Healthcare Consultation
blocks.author: Liu, Zhihuang and Hu, Ling and Zhou, Tongqing and Tang, Yonghao and Cai, Zhiping
blocks.venue: 2025 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy ( SP )
blocks.text: Liu, Zhihuang and Hu, Ling and Zhou, Tongqing and Tang, Yonghao and Cai, Zhiping. (2024). Prevalence Overshadows Concerns? Understanding Chinese Users' Privacy Awareness and Expectations towards LLM-based Healthcare Consultation. 2025 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy ( SP )

fields.title: Prevalence Overshadows Concerns? Understanding Chinese Users' Privacy Awareness and Expectations towards LLM-based Healthcare Consultation
fields.booktitle: 2025 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy ( SP )
fields.author: Liu, Zhihuang and Hu, Ling and Zhou, Tongqing and Tang, Yonghao and Cai, Zhiping
fields.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly gaining traction in the healthcare sector, yet expanding the threat of sensitive health information being easily exposed and accessed without authorization. These privacy risks escalate in regions like China, where privacy awareness is notably limited. While some efforts have been devoted to user surveys on LLMs in healthcare, users' perceptions of privacy remain unexplored. To fill this gap, this paper contributes the first user study (n=846) in China on privacy awareness and expectations in LLM-based healthcare consultations. Specifically, a healthcare chatbot is deployed to investigate users' awareness in practice. Information flows grounded in contextual integrity are then employed to measure users' privacy expectations. Our findings suggest that the prevalence of LLMs amplifies health privacy risks by raising users' curiosity and willingness to use such services, thus overshadowing privacy concerns. 77.3 \% of participants are inclined to use such services, and 72.9 \% indicate they would adopt the generated advice. Interestingly, a paradoxical "illusion" emerges where users' knowledge and concerns about privacy contradict their privacy expectations, leading to greater health privacy exposure. Our extensive discussion offers insights for future LLM-based healthcare privacy investigations and protection technology development.

fields.title: Six Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence Grand Challenges
fields.author: Ozmen Garibay, Ozlem and Winslow, Brent and Andolina, Salvatore and Antona, Margherita and Bodenschatz, Anja and Coursaris, Constantinos and Falco, Gregory and Fiore, Stephen M. and Garibay, Ivan and Grieman, Keri and Havens, John C. and Jirotka, Marina and Kacorri, Hernisa and Karwowski, Waldemar and Kider, Joe and Konstan, Joseph and Koon, Sean and Lopez-Gonzalez , Monica and Maifeld-Carucci , Iliana and McGregor, Sean and Salvendy, Gavriel and Shneiderman, Ben and Stephanidis, Constantine and Strobel, Christina and Ten Holter, Carolyn and Xu, Wei
fields.abstract: Widespread adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies is substantially affecting the human condition in ways that are not yet well understood. Negative unintended consequences abound including the perpetuation and exacerbation of societal inequalities and divisions via algorithmic decision making. We present six grand challenges for the scientific community to create AI technologies that are humancentered, that is, ethical, fair, and enhance the human condition. These grand challenges are the result of an international collaboration across academia, industry and government and represent the consensus views of a group of 26 experts in the field of human-centered artificial intelligence (HCAI). In essence, these challenges advocate for a human-centered approach to AI that (1) is centered in human wellbeing, (2) is designed responsibly, (3) respects privacy, (4) follows human-centered design principles, (5) is subject to appropriate governance and oversight, and (6) interacts with individuals while respecting human's cognitive capacities. We hope that these challenges and their associated research directions serve as a call for action to conduct research and development in AI that serves as a force multiplier towards more fair, equitable and sustainable societies.

blocks.title: Everyday Algorithm Auditing: Understanding the Power of Everyday Users in Surfacing Harmful Algorithmic Behaviors
blocks.author: Shen, Hong and DeVos, Alicia and Eslami, Motahhare and Holstein, Kenneth
blocks.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction
blocks.text: Shen, Hong and DeVos, Alicia and Eslami, Motahhare and Holstein, Kenneth. (2021). Everyday Algorithm Auditing: Understanding the Power of Everyday Users in Surfacing Harmful Algorithmic Behaviors. Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction

fields.title: Everyday Algorithm Auditing: Understanding the Power of Everyday Users in Surfacing Harmful Algorithmic Behaviors
fields.author: Shen, Hong and DeVos, Alicia and Eslami, Motahhare and Holstein, Kenneth
fields.journal: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction
fields.abstract: A growing body of literature has proposed formal approaches to audit algorithmic systems for biased and harmful behaviors. While formal auditing approaches have been greatly impactful, they often suffer major blindspots, with critical issues surfacing only in the context of everyday use once systems are deployed. Recent years have seen many cases in which everyday users of algorithmic systems detect and raise awareness about harmful behaviors that they encounter in the course of their everyday interactions with these systems. However, to date little academic attention has been granted to these bottom-up, user-driven auditing processes. In this paper, we propose and explore the concept of everyday algorithm auditing, a process in which users detect, understand, and interrogate problematic machine behaviors via their day-to-day interactions with algorithmic systems. We argue that everyday users are powerful in surfacing problematic machine behaviors that may elude detection via more centrally-organized forms of auditing, regardless of users' knowledge about the underlying algorithms. We analyze several real-world cases of everyday algorithm auditing, drawing lessons from these cases for the design of future platforms and tools that facilitate such auditing behaviors. Finally, we discuss work that lies ahead, toward bridging the gaps between formal auditing approaches and the organic auditing behaviors that emerge in everyday use of algorithmic systems.

blocks.title: DecodingTrust : A Comprehensive Assessment of Trustworthiness in GPT Models
blocks.author: Wang, Boxin and Chen, Weixin and Pei, Hengzhi and Xie, Chulin and Kang, Mintong and Zhang, Chenhui and Xu, Chejian and Xiong, Zidi and Dutta, Ritik and Schaeffer, Rylan and Truong, Sang T. and Arora, Simran and Mazeika, Manias and Hendrycks, Dan and Lin, Zinan and Cheng, Yu and Koyejo, Sanmi and Song, Dawn and Li, Bo
blocks.venue: Proceedings of the 37th International Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems
blocks.text: Wang, Boxin and Chen, Weixin and Pei, Hengzhi and Xie, Chulin and Kang, Mintong and Zhang, Chenhui and Xu, Chejian and Xiong, Zidi and Dutta, Ritik and Schaeffer, Rylan and Truong, Sang T. and Arora, Simran and Mazeika, Manias and Hendrycks, Dan and Lin, Zinan and Cheng, Yu and Koyejo, Sanmi and Song, Dawn and Li, Bo. fields.title: DecodingTrust : A Comprehensive Assessment of Trustworthiness in GPT Models
fields.booktitle: Proceedings of the 37th International Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems
fields.author: Wang, Boxin and Chen, Weixin and Pei, Hengzhi and Xie, Chulin and Kang, Mintong and Zhang, Chenhui and Xu, Chejian and Xiong, Zidi and Dutta, Ritik and Schaeffer, Rylan and Truong, Sang T. and Arora, Simran and Mazeika, Manias and Hendrycks, Dan and Lin, Zinan and Cheng, Yu and Koyejo, Sanmi and Song, Dawn and Li, Bo
fields.abstract: Generative Pre-trained Transformer (GPT) models have exhibited exciting progress in their capabilities, capturing the interest of practitioners and the public alike. Yet, while the literature on the trustworthiness of GPT models remains limited, practitioners have proposed employing capable GPT models for sensitive applications such as healthcare and finance - where mistakes can be costly. To this end, this work proposes a comprehensive trustworthiness evaluation for large language models with a focus on GPT-4 and GPT-3.5, considering diverse perspectives - including toxicity, stereotype bias, adversarial robustness, out-of-distribution robustness, robustness on adversarial demonstrations, privacy, machine ethics, and fairness. Based on our evaluations, we discover previously unpublished vulnerabilities to trustworthiness threats. For instance, we find that GPT models can be easily misled to generate toxic and biased outputs and leak private information in both training data and conversation history. We also find that although GPT-4 is usually more trustworthy than GPT-3.5 on standard benchmarks, GPT-4 is more vulnerable given jailbreaking system or user prompts, potentially because GPT-4 follows (misleading) instructions more precisely. Our work illustrates a comprehensive trustworthiness evaluation of GPT models and sheds light on the trustworthiness gaps. Our benchmark is publicly available at https://decodingtrust.github.io/.

abstract-1.raw: Generative AI systems now sit in the middle of everyday and professional life: people use them to write, search, code, study, work, and think things through. As people use these systems, they do more than receive outputs. They judge whether responses seem correct, fair, useful, risky, biased, or trustworthy. They decide when to rely on the system, when to question it, when to avoid it, and when to bring it into personal or professional routines. At the same time, researchers, organizations, and practitioners are working out whether generative AI systems are safe, trustworthy, fair, and appropriate for different forms of use.

abstract-2.raw: Much of this evaluation work is treated as a technical process: models are benchmarked, compared, stress-tested, or assessed against a policy or standard. These approaches are necessary, but they do not fully capture how AI systems are evaluated in practice. In real use, evaluation is also done by people. Users notice errors, question sources, test boundaries, compare answers against their expectations, flag things that feel wrong, and make decisions about whether a system should be trusted. These judgments may be informal, incomplete, or uneven, but they matter because they shape how generative AI is adopted, rejected, governed, and improved.

abstract-3.raw: This proposal sets out a dissertation on the human side of generative AI evaluation. It asks how people perceive generative AI systems, how lay users test those systems during direct interaction, how people reflect on their own past AI use, how workplace settings shape decisions about appropriate AI use, and how practitioners approach evaluation as professional work, along with the infrastructure needed to support this work. The central argument is that human-centered evaluation of generative AI is not a single method or study design but a chain of practices that connects user perception, lay auditing, retrospective reflection, workplace governance, practitioner judgment, and reusable research infrastructure.

abstract-4.raw: The completed work begins with a measurement study of user perceptions of trustworthy AI. This study examines trust, fairness, and risk as related but distinct perceptions in the context of generative AI chatbots. Using survey data, factor analysis, and latent class analysis, the study shows that users do not form one uniform public. They differ in how they combine confidence, concern, perceived fairness, trust, and perceived risk. This chapter provides the empirical starting point by showing that before users can audit, reflect on, or govern AI systems, they first interpret those systems through different perception patterns.

abstract-5.raw: The second completed study moves from perception to action. It examines how lay users audit a generative AI chatbot during direct interaction. Participants were asked to look for problematic, questionable, unfair, or biased responses. The study shows that users can identify concerns about trustworthy AI, but naming a concern is not the same as surfacing it. Some participants looked for issues they expected to find but did not uncover them. Others flagged issues based on everyday expectations, personal experience, or interaction style. This work shows both the promise and limits of lay-user auditing: people can contribute meaningful judgments, but they need structured ways to interact with the system, preserve context, mark outputs, explain their reasoning, and produce data that can be analyzed later.

abstract-6.raw: The proposed dissertation includes open-source infrastructure for human-centered AI auditing, now available as a working beta. The tool supports workflows in which participants interact with an AI model, review responses, annotate or evaluate outputs, provide Likert-style ratings and written explanations, and export study data. Its role is to make human-centered evaluation easier to configure, run, and analyze across studies. The remaining work for this contribution is to make the tool more reusable and stable, especially by separating investigator and auditor workflows, improving configuration and documentation, supporting clearer export structures, and preparing the system as a dissertation artifact.

abstract-7.raw: The proposed and underway studies extend the work beyond the original user perception and auditing studies. The AI interaction history reflection study asks what users notice when they review their own accumulated ChatGPT histories and whether this review changes their awareness of sensitive information, perceived benefits and concerns, trust, or intentions for future privacy-protective behavior. The study has received GWU IRB approval and CISPA ERB approval, and the main extension and dashboard workflow have been implemented.

abstract-8.raw: The employee adoption and governance study examines generative AI use in workplace settings, where AI use is not only an individual choice. Employees must decide whether a task is appropriate for AI, whether an output is good enough, whether it needs to be checked, whether AI use should be disclosed, and whether using AI could create risk for others. This interview study examines how employees make these decisions under real organizational conditions, including uncertainty, formal and informal guidance, workplace norms, and task expectations. The study has received the necessary RPO and IRB approvals, and interviews are underway.

abstract-9.raw: The practitioner perspectives study turns to people who design, conduct, support, or rely on AI evaluation work. It asks how practitioners define human-centered evaluation, what methods they use, what evidence they trust, how they interpret human feedback, and what tools or processes are missing. This study connects the user-facing work to the practical conditions under which evaluation is carried out. The study has IRB approval and is in recruitment preparation.

abstract-10.raw: Together, these projects examine generative AI evaluation at successive points where people make sense of system behavior: before use, during interaction, after accumulated use, inside organizations, and in professional evaluation workflows. The expected contributions are fivefold. First, the proposed dissertation contributes an empirical account of how users perceive trust, fairness, and risk in generative AI chatbots. Second, it contributes an empirical account of lay-user auditing and the gap between users' concerns and their ability to surface issues through interaction. Third, it contributes reusable open-source infrastructure for configuring and studying human-centered AI audits. Fourth, it extends human-centered evaluation beyond the single interaction to retrospective reflection on AI histories and workplace adoption and governance. Fifth, it contributes practitioner-facing insight into how human-centered AI evaluation is understood and operationalized in professional practice.

abstract-11.raw: This work matters because generative AI evaluation cannot be left only to benchmarks, technical audits, or high-level governance principles. Those forms of evaluation are important, but they are incomplete without understanding how people actually encounter, judge, use, question, and manage these systems. By studying users, employees, practitioners, and evaluation infrastructure together, the proposed dissertation aims to show how human-centered evaluation can become more systematic, usable, and grounded in real contexts of generative AI use.

block-597aea9c3088cdb0.raw: The central argument is that human-centered evaluation of generative AI is not a single method but a chain of practices, connecting user perception, lay auditing, retrospective reflection, workplace governance, practitioner judgment, and reusable research infrastructure. People form perceptions of a system's trustworthiness, fairness, and risk. They test those perceptions through interaction. Later they may revisit their own history of use and reconsider what they shared, relied on, or would handle differently. At work, the same judgments are shaped by tasks, roles, organizational expectations, and risk to others. And for practitioners, evaluation becomes professional work: deciding what to measure, whose feedback counts, how to read the evidence, and how to connect findings to decisions.

block-461211a4ef52b78a.raw: Because this is a proposal, its projects sit at different stages. Two are complete. The first (Chapter 3) studies trust, fairness, and risk as related but distinct perceptions, and finds that users do not form a single public: they combine confidence, concern, perceived fairness, and perceived risk in different patterns, clustering into groups that read the same system differently. That is the empirical starting point, because before people audit, reflect on, or govern an AI system, they first interpret it. The second (Chapter 4) moves from perception to action, asking how lay users audit a chatbot in direct interaction. It shows both the promise and the limit of lay auditing: people can name real concerns about trustworthiness, but naming a concern is not the same as surfacing it, and doing so takes structured ways to interact, preserve context, mark outputs, explain a judgment, and leave analyzable data behind.

block-12cdd7cf60895f3f.raw: That last finding is what the third project (Chapter 5) responds to. It is open-source infrastructure for human-centered AI auditing, built out of the lay-user study and now running as a working beta: a researcher can configure an evaluation task, have participants interact with a model and judge its responses, and export the results for analysis. The main work left is to make it reusable rather than a one-off, above all by separating an investigator workflow (configuring and previewing a study) from an auditor workflow (completing it without access to the setup). A system is benchmarked, stress-tested, compared against another model, or measured against a policy or standard. That work is necessary, but a growing body of scholarship across HCI, FAccT, CSCW, and usable security argues that it is not sufficient on its own. Trustworthiness, fairness, and risk are not read off a model in isolation; they are produced as people interpret, rely on, contest, and live with these systems in real settings. This chapter reviews that literature in five strands: how trustworthy AI has been reframed as a sociotechnical rather than a purely technical problem; how people perceive and evaluate AI systems through use; how generative AI is evaluated and audited; how AI is taken up and governed in everyday work; and how participatory, human-centered evaluation infrastructure has developed. A sixth strand, on privacy, disclosure, and reflection on AI interaction histories, is outlined at the end and remains to be written. Running through all of them is a single observation: real-world human-AI interaction is itself a site of evaluation and governance, and prior work has only begun to support the situated judgments that happen there.

block-972bcc25dbbe1699.raw: A line of work in FAccT and HCI has argued that trustworthiness cannot be equated with model quality. Selbst et al. show that ``fair'' machine learning routinely fails when it abstracts away the social system an intervention will operate in, naming a set of recurring abstraction traps. Bender et al. make a parallel argument for language models, showing how a scale-first agenda obscures labor, environmental, and representational harms that benchmark-centered narratives leave out. Shelby et al. widen the frame by organizing harms into representational, allocative, quality-of-service, interpersonal, and social-system categories, which makes trustworthiness difficult to reduce to bias metrics alone. Procter et al. reach a similar conclusion from healthcare, arguing that trustworthy AI is better understood as an organizational accountability problem than as a matter of explaining outputs to individual users. Together these papers reposition trustworthy AI as a sociotechnical and organizational concern rather than a technical optimization target.

block-dd87952ccc7baa03.raw: This does not discard technical evaluation so much as relocate it within a broader accountability process. Model documentation matters because it requires developers to state intended use, subgroup performance, and evaluation context rather than presenting a model as context-free \cite{crisanInteractiveModelCards2022}. Work on algorithmic impact assessments goes further, showing that ``impact'' is not something a model has independently of interpretation but is co-constructed through organizational processes and decisions about which downstream effects count. Even as the field adopts richer transparency artifacts, then, trustworthiness still depends on which communities define harms and what review processes surround deployment.

block-fc4af6ccd13ca759.raw: Studies of responsible-AI practice show why this matters concretely: organizational reality tends to exceed what tool-centric pipelines anticipate. Prior work finds that practitioners building fairer systems need support aligned with collaborative workflows, uncertainty, and domain-specific tradeoffs rather than access to fairness metrics alone. Checklist and documentation work similarly shows that abstract principles become usable when translated into review moments and escalation routines that fit actual development practice. Governance, on this evidence, is enacted through review structures and local workflow constraints, and trustworthiness is produced through ongoing interpretation rather than one-time predeployment validation.

block-246a8be8b5c1ee0d.raw: A further strand complicates the assumption that transparency produces appropriate trust. Explanation and interpretability work shows that explanatory interfaces do not reliably curb overreliance and that accuracy, prior interaction, and explanation format interact in nontrivial ways. A related body of work reframes fairness and trust as relational and interpretive: Yurrita et al. show that fairness perceptions depend on contestability and human oversight rather than a single cue \cite{yurritaDisentanglingFairnessPerceptions2023}; Vereschak et al. show that trust in AI-assisted decisions is multi-party, involving those behind the system and those subject to it \cite{vereschakTrustAIassistedDecision2024}; and Schoeffer et al. show that explanations can shift reliance and fairness perceptions without necessarily helping people tell correct advice from incorrect \cite{schoefferExplanationsFairnessAppropriate2024}. Recent work also argues that trust develops across repeated interaction and that human-centered evaluation should attend to the broader capabilities AI enables or constrains over time, not only whether it improved a bounded task metric.

What remains less developed is a coherent account of trustworthiness as something produced and assessed through situated, ongoing human interaction, rather than verified once before release.

heading-0928449e305909a8.label: Section
heading-0928449e305909a8.title: Human Evaluation, Trust, and User Perception of AI Systems

block-22f1234e8f1ee28d.raw: People do not evaluate AI the way researchers evaluate models. Rather than reasoning from internal properties, users form judgments from situated encounters with outputs, interface cues, observed failures, and stories others tell. Early HCI work established this before the current wave by showing that users build partial, adaptive folk theories of what algorithmic systems are doing. Generative AI appears to continue this pattern rather than break it: people develop working theories of model capabilities, harms, and harm-reduction strategies through repeated use rather than from documentation alone. User interpretation, on this view, is part of the sociotechnical system being evaluated, not noise around a ``real'' model.

User interpretation, on this view, is part of the sociotechnical system being evaluated, not noise around a "real" model.

block-0d3787052f5ccde0.raw: A second body of work cautions against treating trust as a simple positive outcome, arguing instead that appropriate reliance is the target. Studies of AI-assisted decision-making show how perceived and actual accuracy shape trust in machine advice, how people respond to erroneous algorithmic scores in the loop, and how cognitive-forcing interventions can reduce overreliance at a usability cost. Ma et al. show that both relative human-AI correctness and a user's own self-confidence shape whether reliance is well calibrated \cite{maWhoShouldTrust2023}. The implication is that trustworthy interaction depends on reasoning well about uncertainty and the division of labor, not on making people feel more positive about a system.

block-da0b3eaed45ef90f.raw: Work on user-facing evaluation and auditing sharpens this point. Users often judge systems by omissions as much as outputs, wanting accounts of what they were not shown as well as explanations of what they were shown. The auditing literature then shows both the promise and the limits of user-driven oversight: Shen et al. argue that everyday users can surface harms that formal audits miss, precisely because they encounter systems in diverse contexts \cite{shenEverydayAlgorithmAuditing2021}. Later work shows this is rarely spontaneous or frictionless and instead depends on scaffolding, coordination, and a division of labor. Real-world use is therefore a critical place where harms become visible, but observing usage is not by itself enough to make those harms legible.

block-4bb17d8387af6004.raw: A fourth strand shows that what counts as a harm is not exhausted by technical metrics or generic satisfaction measures. Gadiraju et al. surface disability-centered perspectives on large language models \cite{gadirajuWouldntSayOffensive2023}; other work studies how users identify stereotypes, perceive algorithmic discrimination, and interpret harms through broader histories of systemic injustice. Participatory work makes the corresponding move on process, showing that affected communities often need to shape the evaluation process itself rather than respond to fixed benchmarks. Generative AI intensifies these concerns because interaction is productive rather than merely diagnostic: Jakesch et al. show that co-writing with opinionated language models can shift users' own views \cite{jakeschCoWritingOpinionatedLanguage2023}, and recent security and safety work shows that people encounter governance through everyday frictions, including uneven content-policy enforcement and safety concerns in personal use contexts.

block-e37311c9bf108a23.raw: This literature provides strong foundations on trust, mental models, explanations, auditing, and harm perception, but it remains fragmented. Trust-calibration studies tend to use short, bounded decision tasks; folk-theory and auditing work shows that users surface real insight in use but only partially and with effort; and harm-perception work is not always connected back to everyday interactional evaluation. What is missing is a connected account that links lived interaction, later reflection, participatory auditing, and organizational oversight.

block-74b7354dc76efdf7.raw: Benchmark-driven evaluation has broadened, but its center of gravity remains the model. Foundational critiques already warned that language-model evaluation is never only about whether a score rises: harms can be obscured by scale-first narratives, data cascades can determine downstream behavior, and functionality can be treated as established independent of context and deployment. Recent generative benchmarks add scale and comparative convenience more than a different theory of evidence, and still tend to treat evaluation as a one-time readout of capability rather than a situated account of behavior in use.

Recent generative benchmarks add scale and comparative convenience more than a different theory of evidence, and still tend to treat evaluation as a one-time readout of capability rather than a situated account of behavior in use.

block-d36d3282a94c5dfd.raw: Human-preference and interactive methods are real progress, yet they do not fully escape benchmark logic. LLM-as-judge approaches, chatbot arenas, and conversational benchmark suites move evaluation toward conversational tasks, pairwise comparison, and real user queries, which recognizes that generative systems are evaluated in interaction. But they still rely on curated prompt sets, platform-specific populations, and proxy judges that compress heterogeneous real-world criteria into tractable scores.

block-93007a0d2476cd8f.raw: Red-teaming, fairness auditing, and privacy and security testing widen the target from accuracy to harm, but often remain episodic and attack-centered. Adversarial Nibbler offers an open red-teaming method for text-to-image models \cite{quayeAdversarialNibblerOpen2024}; other work audits dialect-based quality-of-service harms in chatbots, evaluates whether systems act on privacy norms, demonstrates that training data can sometimes be extracted from language models, and scales jailbreak assessment. This work shows that evaluation is no longer only about task competence, but it usually frames oversight as a bounded event and says less about how harms are perceived, noticed over time, or folded into ordinary governance.

block-9231c07e7c467409.raw: Auditing scholarship shifts attention from models to systems, organizations, and publics. Internal audit frameworks, sociotechnical audits, user-engaged auditing, practitioner accounts of trust and information asymmetry, and arguments about the limits of black-box access together recast evaluation as an organizational and evidentiary process that depends on access, incentives, and interpretive capacity rather than on model probes alone. Participatory and disagreement-aware approaches point toward a more human-centered future while remaining early: user-engaged auditing work foregrounds how people surface situated harms \cite{shenEverydayAlgorithmAuditing2021}, while student and community auditing activities show that non-experts can critically engage with large language model behavior \cite{prabhudesaiHereGPTMade2025}. The clearest unmet need is longitudinal and interactional: human-centered evaluations too often optimize narrow proxy outcomes, and silent model updates can destabilize any one-time evaluation.

It is the literature home for Chapter~\ref{chapter:proposal-ai-histories}, which studies reflection on AI interaction histories. At present, the relevant material appears as a sub-thread across work on privacy perceptions of conversational agents, secret or sensitive use of LLMs, safety perceptions of generative AI conversational agents, and user expectations around AI memory.

block-53cdfbf62d7c7838.raw: Three literatures need to be assembled here. The first is usable privacy and self-disclosure to conversational agents and LLMs, including work on how users decide what to share with chatbots and how they understand privacy risks in conversational interfaces. The second is AI interaction histories and memory as objects of use, including work on what people expect systems to remember and how reviewability changes the meaning of stored interaction traces. The third is personal informatics, self-tracking, and data-driven reflection, which provides a theoretical home for asking what users notice when their own ChatGPT history becomes reviewable.

heading-b97a235b97f12f15.label: Section
heading-b97a235b97f12f15.title: AI Use and Decision-Making in Real-World Contexts

block-4d5d474317f03c2b.raw: Workplace AI adoption is rarely a clean story of acceptance or rejection. Earlier organizational studies already showed that employees resist systems that intensify burden, reduce discretion, or threaten privacy and status. Studies of algorithmic evaluation, frontline decision support, workplace surveillance, and emotion AI reinforce that adoption is mediated by labor conditions and institutional power rather than accuracy alone.

Earlier organizational studies already showed that employees resist systems that intensify burden, reduce discretion, or threaten privacy and status. Studies of algorithmic evaluation, frontline decision support, workplace surveillance, and emotion AI reinforce that adoption is mediated by labor conditions and institutional power rather than accuracy alone.

block-c8555fbd7701ef08.raw: The generative-AI workplace literature extends rather than replaces these concerns. Across knowledge workers, young professionals, teachers, and designers, generative AI is typically framed as assistive, bounded, and subject to human review. Workers imagine generative AI as a tool for routine work under review while worrying about deskilling, dehumanization, disconnection, and disinformation. Other studies connect adoption to identity and accomplishment, showing that productivity gains can coexist with a felt loss of authorship. Teachers, UX professionals, and team-based workers weigh assistive value against creativity, expertise, sensitive-data concerns, and policy uncertainty. Across these studies, workers evaluate AI in use, through situated judgments about task fit, stakes, sensitive data, checkability, and professional legitimacy.

block-4f25114b4f0c75ce.raw: Verification recurs throughout this corpus as a central but under-theorized form of labor. Workers must often verify both AI outputs and the hidden process that produced them. In clinical and organizational decision support, people ignore, trust, or negotiate recommendations depending on actionability and workflow fit, and adoption depends on trust and workflow fit rather than performance alone. Verification is therefore interpretive, often costly, and sometimes socially risky work, and model-centric evaluation rarely captures whether a person can reconstruct, inspect, and decide what to do with an output in context.

block-5ab792838decb77c.raw: A final strand shows that workers are often asked to carry the burden of responsible AI use without commensurate support. Practitioner fairness evaluation is shaped by business imperatives, weak stakeholder engagement, and scaling pressure; AI ethics work is frequently individualized rather than built into durable structures; and knowledge workers often want training on interpretation, misuse, bias, and rights that is inconsistent or absent. Governance, on this evidence, is partly produced in workers' local decisions: when they share or withhold sensitive data, refuse a tool, double-check an output, interpret policy, or escalate a harm.

heading-23868dde0460af6f.label: Section
heading-23868dde0460af6f.title: Participatory and Human-Centered AI Evaluation Infrastructure

block-6e0a02b1f576340e.raw: A first theme in this literature is that practitioners need support not for computing more metrics but for deciding what should count as a meaningful evaluation in context. Fairness tools often miss the realities of industry workflows; even committed teams struggle to select appropriate metrics, identify relevant subgroups, and collect the data needed for disaggregated evaluation; and responsible-AI practice succeeds or fails on organizational structures, incentives, and cross-role coordination rather than method choice alone. Evaluation infrastructure, on this account, must scaffold deliberation, documentation, and coordination around contested constructs, not just host metrics.

block-27294e0e52f55c51.raw: A second theme is the shift from expert-only audits toward participatory and user-engaged auditing. Shen et al. argue that everyday users can surface harms that formal audits miss because those harms emerge in situated use \cite{shenEverydayAlgorithmAuditing2021}; DeVos et al. show that user-driven auditing is not random complaint but involves search strategies, collective interpretation, and hypothesis formation that can be scaffolded; and industry-facing work turns this into a problem of recruiting and motivating participants, structuring reports, and turning user findings into engineering action. This work repositions end users and affected communities from subjects of evaluation to contributors to it.
block-27294e0e52f55c51.text: A second theme is the shift from expert-only audits toward participatory and user-engaged auditing. Shen et al. argue that everyday users can surface harms that formal audits miss because those harms emerge in situated use [shenEverydayAlgorithmAuditing2021]; DeVos et al. show that user-driven auditing is not random complaint but involves search strategies, collective interpretation, and hypothesis formation that can be scaffolded; and industry-facing work turns this into a problem of recruiting and motivating participants, structuring reports, and turning user findings into engineering action. This work repositions end users and affected communities from subjects of evaluation to contributors to it.

block-d1acb661e0157b8b.raw: A third theme is that generative AI intensifies both the need for human participation and the limits of existing workflows. Rastogi et al. build a mixed-initiative system in which people and language models collaborate to generate and organize probes \cite{rastogiSupportingHumanAICollaboration2023}; other work shows that teams relying on language models to evaluate language-model outputs then need ways to validate the validators, because evaluation criteria drift as people inspect outputs. Human-centered generative-AI evaluation, in other words, needs support not only for scoring outputs but for articulating criteria, inspecting variation, comparing models and prompts, and translating evidence into action in ways practitioners can actually use.

block-a38f588036ba3623.raw: A final theme concerns the scope of infrastructure across the lifecycle. Early-stage guidebooks and deliberation tools support multi-stakeholder discussion before a system is built or deployed, foregrounding early decisions about purpose and conditions of use, while assurance-audit frameworks target compliance and external review downstream, emphasizing criteria, procedures, and qualified auditors. These remain poorly integrated, and most systems address one lifecycle stage or one task domain at a time. Used as a comparator, benchmark-hosting infrastructure advances reproducibility and cloud-hosted model comparison, but remains focused on benchmark hosting rather than participatory interpretation, reflection over lived interaction, or collaborative governance.

block-b918e794dd0de446.raw: Prior work has thus shown both that evaluation and governance are sociotechnical practices shaped by organizational constraints and that users and affected stakeholders can meaningfully contribute to auditing, and recent systems add workflows for mixed-initiative probing, evaluator alignment, and domain-specific inspection. These contributions remain fragmented across lifecycle stages, stakeholder groups, and task domains. What the literature still lacks is flexible, modular, and reusable infrastructure that helps diverse participants formulate evaluation criteria, contribute situated evidence from real interaction, reflect on historical outputs and interaction traces, interpret findings together, and turn them into action, rather than treating people as downstream raters of model outputs.

heading-2ee23f3ae1494ab6.label: Chapter
heading-2ee23f3ae1494ab6.title: Measuring User Perceptions of Trustworthy AI

block-e542d60f1c7e311e.raw: Public generative AI chatbots such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and DeepSeek are now used for everyday tasks like information seeking, writing support, brainstorming, summarization, and explanation. As they have become more common, so have concerns about their social and individual effects, especially around privacy, security, manipulation, fairness, bias, and misinformation [57, 21, 14, 30, 59, 20, 31, 36--38, 46, 55, 74]. Those concerns do more than flag possible harms; they shape whether people trust, rely on, avoid, or keep using these systems despite the uncertainty [15, 18, 27]. And skepticism does not necessarily stop use: people may stay concerned and still use a chatbot when it is useful, convenient, or hard to avoid [47, 78].

block-79de9cc583babd4b.raw: Interest in how people respond to these chatbots is growing, but the research remains fragmented. Many studies focus on a specific risk, a particular demographic group, or an isolated feature rather than on how users understand safety-related perceptions more broadly [19, 31, 6, 22, 1], which makes it hard to compare findings or to tell whether people use concepts like trust, fairness, and risk in the same way. A user might distrust a chatbot for giving wrong information, for seeming biased, for mishandling a sensitive topic, or for being opaque about how their data is used: related concerns, but not interchangeable ones.
